meta.blurb: When Temujin's father is poisoned, his clan walks away and leaves the family in poverty. In 1206 the boy is named Genghis Khan, and his riders go on to reach from China to Poland. Here is how, and at what cost.
meta.bible: Genghis Khan: born Temujin about 1162 (year uncertain), elected ruler of all the Mongols in 1206, died 1227 aged about 65; burial place unknown. Temujin: his birth name. Yesugei: Temujin's father, a clan leader, poisoned. Hoelun: Temujin's mother. Borte: Temujin's wife, rescued after being carried off. Jamukha: Temujin's boyhood companion and later rival. Toghrul: an older ruler, Temujin's early ally. Tatars, Merkits, Naimans: rival peoples defeated. Ogedei: Genghis Khan's third son, great khan 1229 to 1241. Toregene: Ogedei's widow, regent. Sorghaghtani Beki: widow of a prince, mother of Mongke, Khubilai and Hulegu. Mongke: great khan 1251 to 1259. Khubilai Khan: great khan from 1260, founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271. Ariq Boke: Khubilai's younger brother and rival. Hulegu: Mongke's brother, took Baghdad in 1258. Batu: grandson of Genghis Khan, led the western campaign of 1236 to 1242. Subutai and Jebe: Mongol generals. Marco Polo: Venetian traveller who left in 1271 and returned in 1295; some scholars doubt parts of his account. The steppe: the grassland of Central Asia. Mongols, Mongolia, Karakorum: the Mongol capital built about 1235. Onon River, Gobi. Kuriltai: the great assembly of 1206. Yassa: the law code, contents uncertain. Yam: relay post system. Paiza: metal passport tablet. Gers: round felt tents. Uyghur: neighbouring people whose script the Mongols borrowed. Secret History of the Mongols: Mongol account written after his death. Western Xia, Jin, Song, Yuan, Ming: Chinese states and dynasties. Khanbaliq: Khubilai's capital, modern Beijing. Beijing, China, Yamen. Khwarazm: empire of the shah in Persia and Central Asia; Otrar: border city where a Mongol caravan was killed in 1218; Bukhara, Samarkand, Tabriz, Maragha. Caspian Sea, Caucasus, Black Sea, Kalka River: a battle in 1223. Cuman: steppe people. Kyiv fell in December 1240. Russia, Poland, Hungary, Sajo River, Europe. Baghdad: fell 1258; Abbasid: the caliph's dynasty. Mamluks: Egyptian rulers; Ain Jalut: battle of 1260. Egypt, Persia, Israel, Middle East, Asia, Mediterranean, India. Golden Horde, Ilkhanate, Chagatai: the other khanates. Japan, Java, Kamikaze. Black Death: plague of the 1340s. Mughal: dynasty of India. Venice, Islam, Muslim, Christian, Buddhist, Daoist. Eternal Blue Sky: the Mongol sky god. Voice and tone: clear, vivid and fair; battles and deaths are stated plainly and without gore; where historians disagree, the text says so; figures are approximate. Added for the full-length book: Borte's father Dei Sechen of the Onggirat; Hoelun's children Khasar, Khachiun, Temuge and Temulun; half-brother Begter; Tayichiud: Yesugei's clan, chief Targutai; Sorqan Shira helped Temujin escape in 1180s; Bo'orchu, Jelme, Muqali: loyal commanders; Subutai joined later; Merkit raid took Borte; Burkhan Khaldun: sacred mountain; Jochi, Chagatai, Ogedei, Tolui: sons of Genghis Khan and Borte; Jochi's birth is uncertain; Baljuna: lake where about nineteen men swore loyalty in 1203; Kereit: Toghrul's people; Senggum: Toghrul's son; Dalan Baljut: battle lost by Temujin about 1189 or 1190; Tata-tonga: Naiman scribe; Shigi Khutukhu: adopted brother, chief judge; Keshig: bodyguard of ten thousand; Tengri: the Eternal Blue Sky; Kuchlug: Naiman prince who took Qara Khitai; Yelu Chucai: Khitan scholar-adviser; Zhongdu: Jin capital, modern Beijing; Kaifeng: Jin capital after 1214; Yehuling: battle of 1211; Juyong Pass; Xi Xia or Western Xia: Tangut kingdom; Caizhou: last Jin city, 1234. Shah Muhammad: ruler of Khwarazm; Inalchuq: governor of Otrar; Urgench, Merv, Nishapur, Parwan, Indus River; Jalal ad-Din: the shah's son; Changchun: Daoist master, met the khan in 1222; Li Zhichang wrote his journey; Jebe and Subutai rode round the Caspian, 1220 to 1223; Derbent, Alans, Georgia, Kalka River. Orkhon River: Karakorum stands there. Batu: grandson of Genghis Khan, led the western campaign; Ryazan, Kolomna, Moscow, Vladimir, Sit River, Kozelsk, Novgorod; Grand Prince Yuri; Dmitr: defender of Kyiv; Volga Bulgars; Sarai: Batu's capital on the Volga; Bela IV: king of Hungary; Henry II: duke of Silesia, killed at Legnica on 9 April 1241; Mohi on 11 April 1241; Sandomierz, Krakow, Pest, Danube, Carpathians, Moravia, Bohemia. Toregene: regent; Guyuk: great khan 1246 to 1248; Oghul Qaimish; John of Plano Carpini; William of Rubruck, Guillaume Boucher: the goldsmith of the silver tree; Louis of France. Hulegu: Ilkhan; Nizari Ismailis (called Assassins), Alamut, Juvayni: Persian historian; al-Musta'sim: last Abbasid caliph in Baghdad, killed 1258; Doquz Khatun: Hulegu's Christian wife; Kitbuqa: Mongol general killed at Ain Jalut on 3 September 1260; Qutuz and Baibars: Mamluk leaders; Aleppo, Damascus, Palestine, Armenia. Berke: Muslim khan of the Golden Horde; Ghazan: Ilkhan who became Muslim in 1295; Ozbeg: Golden Horde khan, Islam official in 1313; Kaidu: rebel prince, died 1301. Khubilai's wife Chabi; Pagpa: Tibetan monk who made the Phags-pa script in 1269; Dadu: Khubilai's new city, same as Khanbaliq; Kaiping; Xiangyang: besieged 1268 to 1273; Lin'an: modern Hangzhou, surrendered 1276; Bayan: Mongol general; Lu Xiufu: Song minister at Yamen, 1279; Guo Shoujing: astronomer and engineer, Shoushi calendar of 1281; Grand Canal; Rustichello: Genoese writer who wrote down Marco Polo's account; Genoa; Rabban Sauma: monk who visited Europe 1287 to 1288; Maragha: observatory founded 1259; Nasir al-Din Tusi: its director; Rashid al-Din: Persian minister who wrote the Compendium of Chronicles about 1300; Jingdezhen: porcelain town; Hu Sihui: wrote the court cookbook of 1330; Hakata Bay: Japan, 1274 and 1281; Tran Hung Dao: Vietnamese general at Bach Dang River, 1288; Dai Viet or Vietnam; Raden Wijaya: founder of Majapahit, 1293; Pagan: Burmese kingdom; Chagatai khanate; Mongolian: the language and people of Mongolia; Toghon Temur: last Yuan emperor in China; Red Turbans: rebels; Zhu Yuanzhang: founder of the Ming in 1368; Northern Yuan; Issyk-Kul: lake in Kyrgyzstan where plague graves of 1338 and 1339 were found; Caffa: Genoese port in Crimea, 1346; Sicily; Timur: Turkic conqueror of Samarkand, defeated the Golden Horde in the 1390s; Tokhtamysh; Ivan III and Akhmat: the standoff on the Ugra River in 1480; Kazan, Astrakhan, Crimea; Babur: founder of the Mughal empire in 1526 at Panipat; Taj Mahal; Delhi; Ulaanbaatar: capital of Mongolia; Naadam: July festival of wrestling, archery and horse racing; Columbus; Soviet Union; Mongolia became a communist state in 1924 and a democracy after 1990.
chapters: A Khan Who Became an Emperor

beats.scene: A lone rider gallops across a vast green grassland under a huge sky
beats.summary: The story opens on the steppe, the sea of grass in Central Asia where the Mongols lived.

beats.scene: Snow covers the plain while a herder in a heavy coat leads his horse
beats.summary: The steppe has extreme weather, with bitter winters and hot, short summers.

beats.scene: A herd of horses, sheep, goats, cattle and camels grazes on a hillside
beats.summary: Mongol herders kept five kinds of animals, and their whole life depended on them.

beats.scene: A round white felt tent on the grass, smoke rising from its roof
beats.summary: Families lived in round felt tents, called gers, that could be packed up and moved quickly.

beats.scene: A woman pours white milk from a leather bag into wooden bowls
beats.summary: Milk, cheese and meat were the staple foods, and mare's milk was fermented into a mild drink.

beats.scene: A long line of carts and animals moves across green hills in summer
beats.summary: Families moved their herds with the seasons to find fresh grass.

beats.scene: A small child sits proudly on a pony while his father walks beside him
beats.summary: Mongol children learned to ride almost as soon as they could walk.

beats.scene: A small, shaggy horse paws through the snow to find the grass beneath
beats.summary: The Mongol horse was small and tough and could survive on the steppe all winter.

beats.scene: Rival camps of herders watch each other warily across a river
beats.summary: There was no Mongol nation yet, only tribes and clans that raided one another and kept blood feuds.

beats.scene: Mountains rise above a plain beneath an enormous, cloudless blue sky
beats.summary: The Mongols honoured the Eternal Blue Sky and lived beside rich, powerful neighbours such as China.

beats.scene: A newborn boy is held up inside a tent beside a river
beats.summary: Temujin, the future Genghis Khan, was born about 1162 near the Onon River to a minor clan leader.

beats.scene: A mother sits with four young children beside a felt tent
beats.summary: Temujin grew up with his mother Hoelun, brothers Khasar, Khachiun and Temuge, and sister Temulun.

beats.scene: A father and a nine-year-old boy ride together across the grassland
beats.summary: At about nine, Temujin was taken to the Onggirat people, promised to Borte and left with her family.

beats.scene: A tired rider is offered a bowl of food at a camp
beats.summary: On the way home Yesugei ate with Tatars and was poisoned; Temujin hurried home but found him dead.

beats.scene: Families pack their tents and drive their herds away, leaving a small camp behind
beats.summary: The Tayichiud clan abandoned Yesugei's widow and children, taking the herds with them.

beats.scene: A woman and her children dig for roots beside a river
beats.summary: Hoelun kept her children alive for years on roots, wild fruit and small fish.

beats.scene: Two boys with bows stand over a dispute among brothers
beats.summary: In a quarrel over food, Temujin and Khasar killed their older half-brother Begter.

beats.scene: A teenage boy wearing a heavy wooden collar is led through a camp
beats.summary: The Tayichiud chief Targutai captured Temujin and made him wear a wooden collar.

beats.scene: A boy in a wooden collar hides in a river among reeds at night
beats.summary: Temujin escaped during a feast, hid in the river, and was helped by a family who did not betray him.

beats.scene: A young man leads a herd of horses across the grass beside a friend
beats.summary: Thieves stole his horses; Temujin tracked them and a stranger named Bo'orchu joined him, the first of many loyal companions.

beats.scene: A young man and a young woman stand together before a felt tent
beats.summary: At about sixteen Temujin went to claim Borte, and they married.

beats.scene: A young man in a splendid fur coat kneels before an older ruler
beats.summary: Temujin gave Borte's sable coat to the powerful ruler Toghrul and asked for his protection.

beats.scene: Riders charge toward a sleeping camp at dawn as people wake in fear
beats.summary: Merkit raiders attacked Temujin's camp at dawn and carried off Borte.

beats.scene: A young man kneels on a forested mountaintop facing the rising sun
beats.summary: Temujin hid on Burkhan Khaldun and thanked the mountain, which the Mongols held sacred, for saving his life.

beats.scene: Two riders on horses talk earnestly as a column of warriors waits behind
beats.summary: Temujin asked Toghrul and his old friend Jamukha for help, and they agreed to raise an army.

beats.scene: Horsemen charge through the dark as a young woman runs toward a rider
beats.summary: The allies attacked the Merkit camp at night, and Temujin and Borte found each other.

beats.scene: A mother holds her baby boy inside a tent
beats.summary: Borte soon gave birth to Jochi, whose true father was uncertain; Temujin accepted him as his son.

beats.scene: Two boys exchange small bones and arrowheads beside a frozen river
beats.summary: Jamukha had been Temujin's boyhood friend and sworn brother, or anda, and they now lived together again.

beats.scene: Two leaders stand apart on a hillside as the camp prepares to move
beats.summary: The two friends parted, probably because they held different ideas about how a leader should rule.

beats.scene: Families follow a banner across the hills as riders join the column
beats.summary: Many people left Jamukha to follow Temujin, which marked the start of the rivalry.

beats.scene: Nobles raise a young man onto a felt carpet in a circle of riders
beats.summary: About 1189 a group of Mongol nobles elected Temujin as their khan.

beats.scene: Two armies clash on a grassy plain below a hill
beats.summary: Jamukha attacked Temujin with a large army, and Temujin lost the battle of Dalan Baljut.

beats.scene: A group of men of different ages and backgrounds kneel before a leader
beats.summary: Temujin rewarded loyalty and skill instead of birth, so talented followers from poor families rose in rank.

beats.scene: Armies of Mongols and northern Chinese soldiers march together against a camp
beats.summary: In 1196 the Jin dynasty asked Temujin and Toghrul to help defeat the Tatars, and gave them titles.

beats.scene: Warriors lay down their weapons and stand in a circle around a leader
beats.summary: He ruled that no man should take loot until the battle was won and that spoils be shared fairly.

beats.scene: A badly wounded leader leans on a companion as a defeated army retreats
beats.summary: In 1203 Toghrul turned against Temujin, and Temujin was badly beaten in a battle in the sands.

beats.scene: A handful of tired men kneel and drink from a muddy pond
beats.summary: Temujin retreated to Lake Baljuna, where, by tradition, a handful of loyal men drank muddy water and swore to stand by him.

beats.scene: Riders swarm down a hillside toward a feasting camp at night
beats.summary: Temujin surprised the Kereit by night in 1203 and defeated them; Toghrul fled and was killed.

beats.scene: A great army fights below a mountain against the Naiman warriors
beats.summary: In 1204 Temujin defeated the Naiman people, the last great rival in the west of Mongolia.

beats.scene: A bound man is brought before a seated leader inside a large tent
beats.summary: Jamukha's own men betrayed him; Temujin punished the traitors and gave his old friend the death he asked for.

beats.scene: Thousands of riders gather before a white standard at a great assembly
beats.summary: In 1206 a great assembly, the kuriltai, named Temujin Genghis Khan beneath a standard of nine white horsetails.

beats.scene: A man in a long robe stands before cheering crowds on the plain
beats.summary: The title's meaning is uncertain; it was probably a word for a strong and universal ruler.

beats.scene: Soldiers in small groups stand in neat lines under different banners
beats.summary: He organised the army in tens, hundreds, thousands and ten thousands, mixing the tribes.

beats.scene: Leaders kneel one by one to receive gifts and titles from a seated khan
beats.summary: He rewarded about ninety-five loyal commanders with command of a thousand men each.

beats.scene: Guards in fine coats stand at the entrance of a large tent at night
beats.summary: He built a bodyguard of ten thousand men, the keshig, which also trained officials and officers.

beats.scene: A judge listens to two herders arguing in front of a tent
beats.summary: A body of law, later called the Yassa, was said to apply to everyone, and it banned kidnapping and theft.

beats.scene: A man in plain clothes writes in a large book while a khan speaks
beats.summary: He appointed his adopted brother Shigi Khutukhu as chief judge to record decisions in writing.

beats.scene: A scholar in a robe writes strange letters on a scroll as boys watch
beats.summary: The Mongols had no writing, so after capturing the Naiman scribe Tata-tonga they adopted the Uyghur script.

beats.scene: Monks, priests and scholars of different faiths sit together in a large tent
beats.summary: The Mongols honoured many religions and excused religious leaders from taxes.

beats.scene: A leader sits with four young men while a woman looks on from behind
beats.summary: Borte and Genghis Khan had four sons, Jochi, Chagatai, Ogedei and Tolui, whose rivalries would shape the empire.

beats.scene: A mounted archer turns in the saddle and shoots at full gallop
beats.summary: The Mongol mounted archer, with a powerful composite bow, was the heart of the army.

beats.scene: A galloping horse with all four hooves in the air, its rider aiming
beats.summary: Riders learned to loose their arrows at the moment when all four hooves were off the ground.

beats.scene: A rider stands in short stirrups to aim a bow over the horse's neck
beats.summary: Stirrups, saddles and endurance let Mongol riders move much faster than the armies they met.

beats.scene: A rider leads a string of spare horses across the plain at dusk
beats.summary: Each soldier had several horses, so the army could travel extremely fast.

beats.scene: A rider chews dried meat while riding, with a leather bag at his saddle
beats.summary: A Mongol soldier carried little: dried meat, dried milk curd and a water bag, and could ride for days without cooking.

beats.scene: Scouts on hills signal to distant riders with flags
beats.summary: Scouts and spies gathered information first, and flags, drums and signals controlled the army in battle.

beats.scene: A small group of riders pretends to flee while others hide behind a hill
beats.summary: Commanders used the trick of the false retreat to draw enemies into an ambush.

beats.scene: A huge ring of riders closes in on animals across an open plain
beats.summary: Great hunts were military training, teaching thousands of riders to move together as a ring.

beats.scene: A commander gives an order while soldiers in small units stand ready
beats.summary: Discipline was strict: orders had to be obeyed at once, and units shared the blame or the praise.

beats.scene: A walled city gate opens as Mongol riders wait outside in the dawn mist
beats.summary: The Mongols offered cities the chance to surrender and spared those who did, and terror itself became a weapon.

beats.scene: Mongol riders cross a desert toward a walled city
beats.summary: From 1205 the Mongols raided Western Xia, a walled kingdom, and found that cities were a new kind of problem.

beats.scene: Water floods a camp of tents beside a broken river dam
beats.summary: In 1209 and 1210 the Mongols besieged the Xia capital and tried to flood it, but the river water flooded their own camp, and Xia agreed to submit.

beats.scene: A smiling ruler in a fine robe kneels before a seated khan
beats.summary: The Uyghurs and other peoples chose to join the Mongols peacefully, bringing skilled scribes and merchants.

beats.scene: Engineers build a tall wooden catapult beside a city wall
beats.summary: Engineers and experts from conquered lands joined the Mongols and built siege machines.

beats.scene: A khan turns his back on a messenger from the Jin court
beats.summary: When the Jin demanded submission, Genghis Khan refused, and in 1211 the Mongols attacked the Jin and won the battle of Yehuling.

beats.scene: Mongol riders pour through a narrow mountain pass toward a great plain
beats.summary: In 1213 the Mongols broke through the Juyong Pass and spread across northern China, and the Jin capital agreed to pay a heavy tribute.

beats.scene: A royal court packs its carts and leaves a city by the south gate
beats.summary: The Jin emperor moved his capital south to Kaifeng; Genghis Khan saw this as breaking the peace, and the old capital fell in 1215.

beats.scene: A scholar in a robe stands before a khan in a tent
beats.summary: Yelu Chucai, a scholar of Khitan descent, joined Genghis Khan and taught him how an empire could use taxes and officials.

beats.scene: A general in armour studies a map beside a river as soldiers camp
beats.summary: In 1217 Genghis Khan left the general Muqali in charge in China, and Muqali kept conquering the north with a small army.

beats.scene: Two horsemen ride into a market town where people welcome them
beats.summary: In 1218 the general Jebe defeated Kuchlug, a Naiman prince who ruled Qara Khitai, and allowed religious freedom there, which the people welcomed.

beats.scene: A shah on a throne in a grand palace greets merchants with gifts
beats.summary: Khwarazm was a rich empire in Persia and Central Asia, and Genghis Khan first tried to open trade with it.

beats.scene: A trade caravan of camels and carts halts at a border town gate
beats.summary: In 1218 a governor at Otrar killed a Mongol trading party, taking its goods.

beats.scene: A khan listens gravely as envoys report on a broken promise
beats.summary: Genghis Khan sent envoys to demand the governor, but the shah killed one and sent the others away.

beats.scene: A khan kneels alone on a mountain top in the wind
beats.summary: Genghis Khan is said to have prayed alone on a mountain for three days before choosing war.

beats.scene: Four columns of riders move through different mountain passes on a map
beats.summary: He divided the army into several columns that attacked the Khwarazmian cities from different directions.

beats.scene: Smoke rises from a great city in a green oasis as riders surround it
beats.summary: In 1220 Bukhara surrendered, but the citadel held out; the city burned and many people died.

beats.scene: Mongol soldiers face the great blue-tiled walls of Samarkand
beats.summary: Samarkand surrendered within a few days in 1220, and thousands of craftsmen were taken to Mongolia.

beats.scene: A lonely, sick man rests in a tent on a rocky island shore
beats.summary: The shah fled before the Mongols and died ill and alone on an island in the Caspian Sea.

beats.scene: Two brothers argue in front of a besieged city while a third steps in
beats.summary: At Urgench in 1221 Jochi and Chagatai quarrelled until Ogedei took command, and the city was destroyed.

beats.scene: A ruined city with broken walls lies silent under a grey sky
beats.summary: In 1221 the cities of Merv and Nishapur were devastated, though the figures given for the dead are disputed.

beats.scene: A young prince on horseback leaps from a high river bank into rushing water
beats.summary: Jalal ad-Din, the shah's son, defeated a Mongol force at Parwan but was caught at the Indus in 1221, where he swam his horse across.

beats.scene: An old monk and companions cross a snowy mountain pass
beats.summary: Genghis Khan invited the Daoist master Changchun, who made a journey of about two years to reach him in 1222.

beats.scene: An elderly monk speaks calmly to a seated khan in a large tent
beats.summary: Changchun told the khan that no medicine could make a man live for ever, and the khan freed Daoist monks from taxes.

beats.scene: Two generals on tired horses ride along a sea shore
beats.summary: Meanwhile Jebe and Subutai were sent to chase the shah and then to explore the lands to the west, an expedition of about three years.

beats.scene: Riders cross a Caucasus pass above a walled seaside town
beats.summary: They crossed the Caucasus mountains by the walled city of Derbent and tricked the Cumans into deserting their allies.

beats.scene: Frightened herders on horseback flee past a river into a land of forests
beats.summary: The defeated Cumans ran into the lands of the Rus, whose princes agreed to meet the Mongols together.

beats.scene: A great Rus army with banners spreads out beside the Kalka River
beats.summary: In May 1223 the Mongols pretended to retreat for days, then turned and defeated the Rus at the Kalka River.

beats.scene: Tired riders in the distance cross a vast empty plain toward the dawn
beats.summary: The generals then rode home, a round trip of thousands of kilometres, and rejoined Genghis Khan.

beats.scene: A khan on horseback leads a long column of riders home across a desert
beats.summary: In 1223 Genghis Khan began the journey home, leaving governors in the conquered cities; his eldest son Jochi died in 1225 or 1227, before his father.

beats.scene: A khan speaks to his four sons in a large tent
beats.summary: Genghis Khan named Ogedei as his heir, partly because Jochi and Chagatai could not agree.

beats.scene: A khan's army marches through a desert toward a distant walled city
beats.summary: In 1226 Genghis Khan attacked Western Xia, which had refused to help in the Khwarazm war.

beats.scene: A horse rears and throws its rider on a wild hunting ground
beats.summary: In 1226 Genghis Khan was thrown from his horse while hunting and fell ill.

beats.scene: Generals stand with bowed heads around a bed inside a tent
beats.summary: Genghis Khan died in August 1227, aged about sixty-five, and the cause of his death is unknown.

beats.scene: A funeral procession of riders moves silently across the grassland
beats.summary: His body was taken home, and his grave was kept secret; it has never been found.

beats.scene: A young prince guards a hearth fire in a large tent while elders talk
beats.summary: Tolui, the youngest son, ruled as regent for two years until the princes could meet.

beats.scene: Princes in rich robes gather in a great tent to choose a new khan
beats.summary: In 1229 the princes elected Ogedei, as Genghis Khan had wished, as the second great khan.

beats.scene: Mongol and Song soldiers attack a city together as a tower burns
beats.summary: In 1234 the Mongols, with help from the Song, destroyed the Jin dynasty and took the whole north of China.

beats.scene: Wooden halls and felt tents rise on a grassy plain with craftsmen working
beats.summary: Around 1235 Ogedei built a capital at Karakorum in the heart of Mongolia.

beats.scene: A scholar presents a bundle of papers to a khan at a long table
beats.summary: Yelu Chucai persuaded Ogedei to tax conquered farmland and order a census, instead of turning farms into pasture.

beats.scene: Princes sit around a map in a tent as scribes take notes
beats.summary: At the assembly of 1235 the Mongols decided on new wars in Korea, southern China and the west.

beats.scene: A young prince and an old general study a map beside a campfire
beats.summary: In 1236 Batu, a grandson of Genghis Khan, and the veteran general Subutai led a great army to the west.

beats.scene: A town on a great river burns while riders wait on the far bank
beats.summary: In 1236 and 1237 the Mongols crushed the Volga Bulgars and the Cumans, who stood in their way.

beats.scene: A frozen river curves through a snowy forest as riders gallop on the ice
beats.summary: The Mongols attacked the Rus lands in winter, when the frozen rivers served as roads.

beats.scene: A walled wooden town burns at night as snow falls
beats.summary: In December 1237 Ryazan refused to surrender and fell after a few days of attack.

beats.scene: A wooden fortress above a river as Mongol riders approach in the snow
beats.summary: In early 1238 the Mongols took Kolomna and Moscow, then a small town, and moved on to Vladimir.

beats.scene: Domed churches and white walls of a great city burn under a winter sky
beats.summary: Vladimir fell in February 1238, after its Grand Prince left to raise an army.

beats.scene: A battle on a snowy riverbank where Mongol riders surround a Rus army
beats.summary: On 4 March 1238 the Mongols defeated and killed Grand Prince Yuri at the Sit River.

beats.scene: A small wooden town on a hill holds out against a large army
beats.summary: Kozelsk, a small town, resisted for about seven weeks in spring 1238, and the Mongols turned back before the spring thaw.

beats.scene: A walled city on a hill above a wide river before a huge army
beats.summary: After resting, the Mongols attacked again in 1239 and 1240, and Kyiv fell in December 1240.

beats.scene: A tax collector writes in a ledger beside a map of a vast land
beats.summary: Rus princes became vassals of the Golden Horde, paying tribute for over two centuries; historians debate how harsh this rule was.

beats.scene: A king on a throne receives refugees in felt coats and fur hats
beats.summary: Hungary sheltered the Cumans who had fled the Mongols, and the Mongols treated this as a reason for war.

beats.scene: Columns of riders cross snowy mountain passes from several directions
beats.summary: In early 1241 the Mongols attacked Poland and Hungary at the same time, from several directions.

beats.scene: Flames rise over a Polish town as people flee along a snowy road
beats.summary: The Mongol force in Poland raided Sandomierz and Krakow, and the Polish princes fled.

beats.scene: Knights in armour charge across a field as smoke drifts and riders circle
beats.summary: On 9 April 1241 the Mongols defeated the army of Duke Henry II at Legnica, and Henry was killed.

beats.scene: Hungarian soldiers sleep in a fortified wagon camp beside a river at night
beats.summary: On 11 April 1241 the Mongols crossed the Sajo River by night and defeated the Hungarians at Mohi.

beats.scene: A king escapes over a rocky coast to a small island by boat
beats.summary: King Bela escaped, the city of Pest was burned, and the Mongols overran Hungary during 1241.

beats.scene: A messenger gallops into a camp through the snow with a sealed letter
beats.summary: Ogedei died in Karakorum in December 1241, and the news of his death reached the army in the spring.

beats.scene: Mongol riders turn their horses east across a muddy plain at dawn
beats.summary: In 1242 the Mongols left Hungary; historians still debate why, but the death of Ogedei was probably central.

beats.scene: A tent city with a rich palace tent stands beside a wide river
beats.summary: Batu settled on the Volga River and founded a capital called Sarai, which became the heart of the Golden Horde.

beats.scene: A pope reads a letter by candlelight while monks take notes
beats.summary: Europe was shocked, and the pope sent envoys to the Mongol court.

beats.scene: A noblewoman in a fine robe holds court in a large tent
beats.summary: Ogedei's widow Toregene ruled as regent for about five years after his death.

beats.scene: A woman in a long headdress directs servants beside carts and herds
beats.summary: Mongol noblewomen held real power: they ran camps and herds, held property and had a voice in politics.

beats.scene: A great tent city with thousands of guests gathers for a royal ceremony
beats.summary: In 1246 Guyuk was elected great khan at an enormous assembly, which the friar Plano Carpini attended.

beats.scene: A sick ruler is carried in a litter along a dusty road
beats.summary: Guyuk ruled for only two years and died in 1248, perhaps while preparing to confront Batu.

beats.scene: A mother in a plain robe teaches four young sons beside a cradle
beats.summary: Sorghaghtani Beki, widow of Tolui, was a Christian princess who raised four sons who would rule great lands.

beats.scene: Princes raise a new khan on a felt carpet beside a river
beats.summary: In 1251 Batu and Sorghaghtani Beki helped Mongke become great khan, and he then punished many of his rivals.

beats.scene: Clerks with brushes count people and animals while a khan watches
beats.summary: Mongke ordered a census, set fairer and more regular taxes, and tried to reduce corruption.

beats.scene: A traveller in a plain brown robe walks among tents in a dusty yard
beats.summary: In 1254 William of Rubruck, a friar sent by the French king, reached Karakorum and described it.

beats.scene: A great silver tree with four lions pours drinks into silver bowls
beats.summary: In the palace stood a silver tree, made by a French goldsmith named Guillaume Boucher, that poured drinks from its branches.

beats.scene: Priests, monks and scholars sit in a circle as a khan listens
beats.summary: In 1254 Mongke held a debate among Christians, Muslims and Buddhists, and he said that there are many paths to one God.

beats.scene: A khan points to two distant regions on a large map
beats.summary: Mongke planned two great campaigns, against the Song in China and against the Muslim lands in the west.

beats.scene: A high mountain fortress stands against a stormy sky with an army below
beats.summary: In 1256 Hulegu took the mountain fortresses of the Nizari Ismailis, whose castle at Alamut had been feared for generations.

beats.scene: An envoy in the Mongol court holds a letter before a nervous caliph
beats.summary: Hulegu demanded that the Abbasid caliph of Baghdad submit; the caliph refused, believing his city could not fall.

beats.scene: Mongol soldiers and engineers surround a round-walled city by two rivers
beats.summary: In January 1258 Mongol columns surrounded Baghdad and bombarded its walls for about two weeks.

beats.scene: Smoke rises over a great city beside a river as soldiers enter the gates
beats.summary: Baghdad was sacked for about a week in February 1258, and the caliph was executed; the numbers killed are debated.

beats.scene: Christian and Muslim families walk safely out of a church and a mosque
beats.summary: Some Christians were spared, partly through Hulegu's Christian wife Doquz Khatun, and many libraries were damaged, though the extent of the loss is debated.

beats.scene: Mongol riders enter a walled Syrian city as people watch from rooftops
beats.summary: In 1260 Mongol forces took Aleppo and Damascus in Syria, aided by Christian allies from Armenia and Georgia.

beats.scene: A messenger hands a sealed letter to a commander at a mountain camp
beats.summary: In 1259 Mongke died during the war in China, and Hulegu pulled most of his army back, leaving a small force in Syria.

beats.scene: Armoured horsemen face each other across a valley beside a spring
beats.summary: On 3 September 1260 the Mamluks of Egypt beat a Mongol force at Ain Jalut, the first big Mongol defeat in the west.

beats.scene: Two armies on opposite sides of a river with banners flying
beats.summary: The Mongols never advanced further into Egypt, as Hulegu was soon drawn into a war with his cousin Berke of the Golden Horde.

beats.scene: A young prince in a fine robe reads a scroll with Chinese scholars
beats.summary: Khubilai, a grandson of Genghis Khan, was curious about China and gathered Chinese and Tibetan advisers.

beats.scene: Two khans at rival ceremonies hold banners in two different cities
beats.summary: When Mongke died, both Khubilai and his brother Ariq Boke were declared great khan in 1260, in different places.

beats.scene: Armies of two brothers face each other across a wide grassy valley
beats.summary: In a war from 1260 to 1264, Khubilai defeated Ariq Boke by cutting off the grain supply to Karakorum.

beats.scene: Masons and carpenters build a vast walled city on a flat plain
beats.summary: From 1267 Khubilai built a new capital, Khanbaliq, in a regular grid, on the site of modern Beijing.

beats.scene: A ceremony of officials in Chinese robes beside altars of ancestors
beats.summary: In 1271 Khubilai named his dynasty Yuan, from an ancient Chinese book, and claimed to rule as a Chinese emperor.

beats.scene: A scribe in a government office with four groups of people waiting in line
beats.summary: Khubilai's government favoured Mongols and their allies, and Chinese people of the south had the fewest rights.

beats.scene: A great siege engine hurls stones at a city wall across a river
beats.summary: From 1268 to 1273 the Mongols besieged the Song city of Xiangyang, and Persian engineers built giant machines that broke the defence.

beats.scene: A boy emperor and an empress dowager hand a seal to a Mongol general
beats.summary: In 1276 the Song capital Lin'an surrendered without being sacked, under the general Bayan.

beats.scene: A fleet of ships burns in a sea battle near a rocky coast
beats.summary: In 1279 the last Song resistance ended at Yamen, and all of China came under Mongol rule.

beats.scene: Barges full of grain move along a canal toward a walled capital
beats.summary: Khubilai improved roads, canals and the Grand Canal, to carry grain from the south to the new capital.

beats.scene: A map of Asia and Europe with a caravan route across the whole continent
beats.summary: In the late 1200s a traveller could cross Asia from China to the Black Sea within lands ruled by Mongols; this was later called the Mongol Peace.

beats.scene: A rider hands a message to a fresh rider at a post station
beats.summary: The yam relay system carried messages and officials across the empire at great speed.

beats.scene: A traveller holds up a small metal tablet as guards wave him through
beats.summary: A metal tablet called a paiza served as a passport and gave the holder the right to food, horses and lodging.

beats.scene: Guards stand beside a road while merchants pass with loaded carts
beats.summary: Roads were policed, and local officials were made responsible for thefts in their districts.

beats.scene: Camels loaded with silk bales and spices pass through a crowded market
beats.summary: Trade across Asia boomed, carrying silk, spices, silver, porcelain and horses.

beats.scene: A merchant hands over a paper banknote stamped with a red seal
beats.summary: The Yuan government printed paper money, which amazed visitors but later lost value.

beats.scene: A young Venetian merchant in a fur-trimmed coat speaks with a seated khan
beats.summary: Marco Polo left Venice in 1271 with his father and uncle and reached Khubilai Khan's court around 1275.

beats.scene: A great ship leaves a Chinese harbour carrying a princess
beats.summary: Marco Polo returned by sea in 1291, escorting a Mongol princess to Persia, and reached Venice in 1295.

beats.scene: A prisoner dictates to a writer at a small desk
beats.summary: Marco Polo dictated his account to a writer in a Genoese prison, but some scholars still doubt parts of the story.

beats.scene: A monk in a plain robe stands before a king in a European palace
beats.summary: Rabban Sauma, a monk born near Khanbaliq, was sent by a Mongol ruler of Persia to visit European kings in 1287 and 1288.

beats.scene: Scholars of different countries talk together around a table of books and instruments
beats.summary: Mongol courts brought together scholars, doctors and craftsmen from China, Persia, Tibet and Europe.

beats.scene: A domed observatory on a hill with astronomers using large brass instruments
beats.summary: In 1259 Hulegu founded an observatory at Maragha in Persia, where the scholar Nasir al-Din Tusi worked with astronomers from several lands.

beats.scene: A tall stone observatory stands in a courtyard while Chinese astronomers measure shadows
beats.summary: Under Khubilai, the astronomer Guo Shoujing built instruments and made the Shoushi calendar of 1281 with a year of 365.2425 days.

beats.scene: A doctor feels a patient's wrist while another reads a medical book
beats.summary: Persian and Chinese doctors shared medical ideas, and Rashid al-Din had Chinese medical texts translated into Persian.

beats.scene: A scholar writes at a desk surrounded by scrolls from many countries
beats.summary: Rashid al-Din wrote a vast history of the world, the Compendium of Chronicles, with help from experts from many countries.

beats.scene: A potter paints blue designs on a white vase in a workshop
beats.summary: Chinese potters used cobalt from Persia to make blue-and-white porcelain, which became popular across Asia.

beats.scene: Officials in Persia look at paper notes with Chinese characters on a table
beats.summary: In 1294 the ruler of Persia tried to introduce paper money on the Chinese model, but the experiment failed within weeks.

beats.scene: A soldier lights a fuse on a pottery bomb beside a catapult
beats.summary: The Mongols used gunpowder weapons they met in China, and the knowledge of them probably spread westward.

beats.scene: A scribe paints a square script in vertical columns on a seal
beats.summary: In 1269 Khubilai ordered the Tibetan monk Pagpa to design a script to write all the languages of the empire.

beats.scene: A cook in a palace kitchen stirs a pot with spices from many places
beats.summary: A cookbook of 1330 written for the Yuan court listed dishes and ingredients from many lands.

beats.scene: Hundreds of ships approach a rocky bay with samurai waiting on the shore
beats.summary: In 1274 Khubilai sent a fleet against Japan, which landed at Hakata Bay but withdrew after a day of fighting and a storm.

beats.scene: Workers pile stones into a long wall along a sandy shore
beats.summary: The Japanese built a stone wall around Hakata Bay to defend against the next attack.

beats.scene: A huge fleet is tossed by a typhoon as waves break over the ships
beats.summary: In 1281 a far larger invasion was wrecked by a typhoon, a storm the Japanese later called kamikaze, the divine wind.

beats.scene: A narrow river at low tide, sharp stakes in the mud, ships stuck
beats.summary: In Vietnam the Tran dynasty defeated the Mongols several times, most famously by planting stakes in the Bach Dang River in 1288.

beats.scene: A fleet unloads soldiers in a tropical harbour with palm trees
beats.summary: In 1293 a Mongol expedition to Java was tricked into helping a local prince and then driven out.

beats.scene: A column of soldiers and horses struggles through a steaming forest
beats.summary: In tropical lands, such as Burma and Vietnam, the Mongol horse army was much less effective.

beats.scene: An old khan sits alone in a quiet palace room by a lamp
beats.summary: Khubilai Khan died in 1294, after sorrows in his family, aged about seventy-eight.

beats.scene: A map of Asia divided into four large regions, each with its own banner
beats.summary: By then the empire had split into four khanates: the Yuan, the Golden Horde, the Ilkhanate and the Chagatai.

beats.scene: A ruler in a turban kneels to pray in a mosque with courtiers
beats.summary: Several Mongol rulers, including Berke, Ghazan and Ozbeg, became Muslims and made Islam important in their lands.

beats.scene: Mongol nobles in Chinese silk robes and Persian turbans share a feast
beats.summary: Over time the Mongol rulers took on the languages and customs of the lands they ruled and lost their own.

beats.scene: A weary official counts empty grain bins while farmers wait outside
beats.summary: In the 1300s the Yuan dynasty was weakened by quarrels at court, inflation and a series of floods and famines.

beats.scene: A crowd of peasants with red headscarves marches along a country road
beats.summary: From 1351 the Red Turban rebellions spread across China, and one rebel leader, Zhu Yuanzhang, rose to power.

beats.scene: A new emperor on a throne as Mongol officials leave the gate
beats.summary: In 1368 Zhu Yuanzhang founded the Ming dynasty, and the Yuan court fled north from Khanbaliq.

beats.scene: A small lake in high mountains with an old gravestone and a few tents
beats.summary: A new plague, the Black Death, probably began in Central Asia, and a 2022 study found plague DNA in graves from 1338 and 1339 near Lake Issyk-Kul.

beats.scene: Horsemen besiege a walled port while ships wait in the harbour
beats.summary: In 1346 a Golden Horde army besieged the Genoese port of Caffa, where plague broke out; ships from Caffa carried the disease to Europe in 1347.

beats.scene: A ship docks as people on the quay watch sick sailors
beats.summary: In 1347 plague reached Sicily and the Italian ports, then spread across Europe, killing perhaps a third or more of the people.

beats.scene: A governor on horseback looks at a map divided into broken pieces
beats.summary: The Ilkhanate in Persia had already collapsed in 1335, and the other khanates also broke into smaller states.

beats.scene: A conqueror with a map sits beside a young khan on a throne
beats.summary: In the late 1300s Timur, a Turkic conqueror from Samarkand, ruled in the name of Mongol khans and crushed the Golden Horde.

beats.scene: A huge Russian army faces a smaller Tatar force across a frozen river
beats.summary: In 1480 Ivan III of Moscow stood against the Golden Horde's successors on the Ugra River, ending their claim to rule Russia.

beats.scene: A young prince on horseback looks over a plain of armies
beats.summary: In 1526 Babur, who counted Timur and Genghis Khan among his ancestors, founded the Mughal Empire in India.

beats.scene: A ruined town with empty fields lies beside a half-rebuilt canal
beats.summary: The conquests killed very many people, but historians disagree widely about how many.

beats.scene: A broken underground canal in a dry field with an abandoned village
beats.summary: In some regions, such as parts of Persia and Central Asia, irrigation works were wrecked and recovery took generations.

beats.scene: A medieval map of Asia and Europe beside a scholar reading a travel book
beats.summary: The empire also connected distant peoples; Marco Polo's book was read by Columbus and many others.

beats.scene: A scholar studies an old manuscript with Mongol writing by lamplight
beats.summary: The Secret History of the Mongols, written in the thirteenth century, is the main Mongol source on Genghis Khan and does not hide his faults.

beats.scene: A laboratory scientist holds up a glass tube beside a map of Asia
beats.summary: A 2003 genetic study found that a single male line is carried by about eight in every hundred men across a huge region of Asia, perhaps linked to Genghis Khan's family.

beats.scene: A statue of a leader is covered with a cloth in a snowy square
beats.summary: In the Soviet era Mongolia discouraged the praise of Genghis Khan, and after 1990 his memory returned.

beats.scene: A giant steel statue of a horseman stands on a green hill
beats.summary: Today a huge statue of Genghis Khan stands east of Ulaanbaatar, and the main airport carries his name.

beats.scene: A family with a herd of horses outside a white felt tent at sunset
beats.summary: Many Mongolians still live as herders in gers, and the Naadam festival keeps wrestling, archery and horse racing alive.

beats.scene: A map showing Poland, Russia, Iran, Iraq and China with old walls and ruins
beats.summary: In the lands that the Mongols attacked, such as Iran, Iraq, Russia, Ukraine and China, the memory of the conquests is painful.

beats.scene: A herder on horseback rides toward a statue on a distant hill
beats.summary: The story ends on two truths: the Mongols connected the world and wounded it, and every generation must weigh them again.

A1A2: Mongolia is a huge land of grass, wind and open sky.
In winter it is very, very cold, and snow covers the land.
Families kept horses, sheep, goats, cows and camels on the grass.
They lived in round tents made of thick felt.
They ate meat and cheese, and they drank a lot of milk.
When the grass was gone, the families moved to a new place.
Children learned to ride horses when they were very small.
The Mongol horse was small, but it was strong and tough.
There was no Mongol nation, only many tribes that fought each other.
The Mongols loved the sky, which they called Eternal Blue Sky.
A boy called Temujin was born on the grass long ago.
He had three brothers and a sister, and his mother was Hoelun.
When Temujin was nine, his father took him to find a wife.
Yesugei ate bad food on the road home, and soon he died.
The clan left Temujin's family alone, and took the animals.
Hoelun found roots and berries, and the children fished in the river.
The brothers had a bad fight over food, and one died.
Enemies caught Temujin and put a wooden collar around his neck.
One night Temujin ran away and hid in the cold river.
Thieves took his horses, but a young man named Bo'orchu helped him.
Years later, Temujin went back to find Borte, and they married.
Borte's mother gave them a very fine and costly fur coat.
At dawn, enemy riders attacked his camp and took Borte.
Temujin hid on a mountain, and he thanked it for his life.
Temujin asked two strong friends to help him get Borte back.
Borte heard his voice in the dark, and she ran to him.
Soon Borte had a baby boy, and he was called Jochi.
They were friends from childhood, and they stayed together again.
One day the two friends decided that they should part.
Many people left Jamukha, and they followed Temujin instead.
In about 1189, some leaders chose Temujin to be their khan.
Jamukha attacked with a big army, and Temujin lost the battle.
Temujin chose his helpers for their skill, not for their family.
In 1196, the Jin rulers asked Temujin to fight the Tatars.
Temujin made a rule that nobody could take things until the fight ended.
Toghrul turned against him, and Temujin lost a big fight.
At Baljuna, a few faithful men drank muddy water with him.
Temujin attacked the Kereit by surprise and won a great victory.
In 1204, he beat the Naimans, who were strong enemies.
At last, Jamukha's own men took him to Temujin.
In 1206, the people gave Temujin a new name, Genghis Khan.
Nobody is sure what the name Genghis really means.
He put the army into groups of ten, a hundred and more.
He gave rewards to his most loyal friends and helpers.
He chose ten thousand men to guard him day and night.
He made laws that were the same for everyone.
He chose a wise judge to write down the decisions.
The Mongols began to write their words with a new script.
The Mongols were kind to people of many different religions.
He had four sons, and they were all very different.
Mongol soldiers used strong bows, and they rode horses very well.
They shot their arrows at exactly the right moment.
Mongol armies could ride much faster than the armies they fought.
Each soldier had several horses, so he could change when tired.
A soldier carried dried meat, dried milk and a bag of water.
Scouts rode ahead to learn about the enemy first.
Some riders pretended to run away, and the enemy chased them.
Big hunts taught the soldiers how to work together as a team.
The soldiers obeyed orders at once, and they never ran away.
Cities that gave up quickly were often left in peace.
In 1205, the Mongols attacked a land with strong walled cities.
A flood hit the Mongol camp, but the Xia king gave up.
The Uyghurs joined the Mongols, and they were not attacked.
Engineers joined the Mongols and built tall machines to throw stones.
The Jin asked Genghis Khan to bow, but he said no.
In 1213, the Mongols rode through a pass and spread over northern China.
The Jin emperor ran south, and the Mongols took his capital.
A wise man named Yelu Chucai joined Genghis Khan after that.
Genghis Khan left a great general, Muqali, in charge in China.
In 1218, Jebe drove out a cruel ruler, and people were glad.
West of the Mongols lay Khwarazm, a rich land with big cities.
In 1218, a governor at Otrar killed a group of Mongol traders.
Genghis Khan asked for justice, but the shah killed his messenger.
Genghis Khan went to a mountain to pray for three days.
He split his army into groups, and they marched different ways.
In 1220, the Mongols took Bukhara, and a big fire began.
A month later, the Mongols reached the great city of Samarkand.
The shah ran away, and he died alone on an island.
At Urgench, two brothers argued, and a third took command.
Merv and Nishapur were destroyed, and many people died.
The shah's son fought bravely, then jumped his horse into a wide river.
Genghis Khan asked a wise old monk to come and visit him.
The monk told him that no medicine can make people live forever.
Two generals took a small army and rode far to the west.
They crossed high mountains, and they met a new enemy.
The Cumans ran away, and the Rus princes made a plan.
The Mongols pretended to run away, then turned and attacked.
After the victory, the generals rode a long way home.
Genghis Khan went home, and he was tired after the long war.
He chose his son Ogedei to rule after him.
In 1226, Genghis Khan went to war with Western Xia again.
One day he fell from his horse, and he became ill.
In 1227, Genghis Khan died, and the cause is not known.
His body was taken home, and the grave was kept secret.
His youngest son, Tolui, ruled for two years until a new khan was chosen.
In 1229, the princes chose Ogedei as the new great khan.
In 1234, the Mongols and the Song destroyed the Jin.
Ogedei built a new city called Karakorum in the middle of Mongolia.
Yelu Chucai told Ogedei to tax the farms, not destroy them.
In 1235, the princes made plans for many new wars.
In 1236, a huge army left to attack the lands in the west.
First the Mongols destroyed the Bulgars and the Cumans.
They came in winter, when the rivers were frozen hard.
In December 1237, the Mongols attacked and destroyed Ryazan.
After that, they took Kolomna and a small town called Moscow.
In February 1238, Vladimir fell to the Mongols.
A month later, the Mongols defeated Prince Yuri's army.
A small town held out for seven weeks against the army.
After a rest, the Mongols came back and attacked again.
For a long time, the Rus princes had to pay the Mongols.
The Cumans ran to Hungary, and the king let them stay.
In 1241, the Mongols attacked Poland and Hungary together.
In Poland, the Mongols burned towns, and the princes ran away.
On 9 April 1241, the Mongols beat the Polish army near Legnica.
Two days later, the Mongols fought the Hungarians by a river.
The king ran away, and the Mongols took Hungary.
In December 1241, the great khan Ogedei died far away.
In 1242, the Mongols rode home, and nobody knows exactly why.
Batu stayed in the west, and his lands became the Golden Horde.
Europe was shocked, and the Pope sent messengers to the Mongols.
After Ogedei died, his wife, Toregene, ruled the empire.
Mongol women worked hard, and some of them held great power.
In 1246, her son Guyuk became the new great khan.
Guyuk ruled for two years, and then he died.
Sorghaghtani Beki, a clever woman, raised four sons who became rulers.
In 1251, her son Mongke became the great khan.
Mongke ordered all people and animals to be counted for taxes.
In 1254, a monk from Europe reached Karakorum and wrote about it.
In the palace stood a silver tree that poured out drinks.
Mongke listened as priests of three religions argued about their faiths.
Mongke made big plans for two new wars.
In 1256, Hulegu took the mountain castle of Alamut.
Hulegu told the ruler of Baghdad to obey him.
In January 1258, the Mongols surrounded Baghdad with a huge army.
The Mongols entered Baghdad, and many people died there.
Hulegu's wife was a Christian, and she helped some people.
In 1260, Mongol armies took the cities of Aleppo and Damascus.
Then news came that the great khan Mongke had died.
In 1260, the Mamluks of Egypt beat the Mongols at Ain Jalut.
The Mongols did not go any farther toward Egypt after that.
Khubilai was a grandson of Genghis Khan who loved learning.
In 1260, two brothers each said that he was the great khan.
The brothers went to war, and Khubilai won in the end.
Khubilai built a great new capital where Beijing is today.
In 1271, he gave his government a Chinese name, Yuan.
The Mongols gave more power to Mongols than to Chinese people.
The Mongols attacked the Song city of Xiangyang for five years.
In 1276, the Song capital gave up without a fight.
In 1279, the last Song fleet was destroyed at sea.
Khubilai built roads and canals to bring food to the capital.
For the first time, people could travel across Asia more safely.
Riders carried messages from station to station across the empire.
A small metal tablet worked like a passport on the roads.
The roads were watched, so thieves were not safe.
Traders carried silk, spices and silver from one place to another.
The Yuan government printed paper money, and visitors were amazed.
A young man named Marco Polo travelled from Venice to China.
Marco Polo went home by sea and reached Venice in 1295.
In prison, Marco Polo told his story to another man.
A monk from China visited the kings of Europe.
Mongol rulers invited clever people from many countries to their courts.
Hulegu built a big observatory for studying the stars.
Chinese and Persian scientists worked together on the study of the sky.
Doctors from different lands shared what they knew about medicine.
Rashid al-Din wrote a history of the whole world.
Chinese potters made blue and white pots for far countries.
In 1294, Persia tried to use paper money, but it failed.
The Mongols used fire weapons that they learned about in China.
Khubilai asked for one script to write every language of his empire.
A cook book from the Yuan court had foods from many lands.
In 1274, Khubilai sent a fleet to attack Japan.
The Japanese built a long stone wall along the shore.
In 1281, a huge storm destroyed most of the Mongol ships.
In Vietnam, the Mongols were beaten again and again.
In 1293, a Mongol army sailed to the island of Java.
In hot, wet forests, Mongol horses were not very useful.
In 1294, the old Khubilai Khan died in his palace.
By then, the empire was divided into four big parts.
Many Mongol rulers in the west became Muslims.
Over time, the Mongols began to live like the people they ruled.
In the 1300s, the Yuan rulers in China grew weak.
In 1351, farmers in China began to fight the Yuan.
In 1368, Zhu Yuanzhang became emperor, and the Mongols left.
In the 1330s, a terrible illness began in Central Asia.
In 1346, a Mongol army attacked the trading port of Caffa.
In 1347, the sickness reached Europe by ship.
The Mongol states were breaking into smaller pieces.
Timur, a new conqueror, rose up in Central Asia.
In 1480, Moscow refused to pay the Mongol khan any more.
In 1526, a prince named Babur began a new empire in India.
The Mongol wars killed a very large number of people.
In some places, farms and water channels were ruined for years.
The Mongol empire also brought distant people closer together.
A very old Mongol book tells the story of Genghis Khan.
Scientists found one family line in many men across Asia.
For many years, Mongolia did not praise Genghis Khan in public.
Today a huge steel statue of Genghis Khan stands on a hill.
Many Mongolian families still live in tents and keep animals.
In other lands, people remember the Mongol attacks with sadness.
Today, Mongolia honours Genghis Khan as its most famous leader.
B1B2: Far to the north of China lies the steppe, a sea of grass that stretches for thousands of kilometres. Few trees grow there, and the wind blows almost without stopping.
Winter temperatures on the steppe can fall to about minus forty degrees, cold enough to freeze a bucket of milk solid. Summers are short and hot, and a dry year can leave the grass thin and brown.
Mongol families kept five kinds of animals, which were horses, sheep, goats, cattle and camels. Each kind had its own use, and together they gave a family nearly everything it needed.
Their homes were round tents called gers, made of a wooden frame covered with thick sheets of felt. A family could take one down in an hour and load it on a cart, so home could always move.
Most of their food came from their animals, such as meat, milk, yoghurt and hard dried cheese. They also fermented mare's milk into a mild, sour drink that they could carry on long journeys.

Because the animals ate the grass quickly, families could never stay in one place for long. They spent the winter in sheltered valleys and moved to the open plains in summer, following the fresh pasture.

Mongol children began to ride at about the age of three, sometimes tied to the saddle to keep them safe. By the time they were teenagers, they could ride, hunt and shoot an arrow while the horse was running.
The Mongol horse was smaller than the horses of Europe, with a thick coat and a strong back. It could find its own food, even in deep snow, by scraping the ground with its hooves.

In those days the steppe had no single ruler, only many tribes and clans such as the Mongols, Tatars, Kereit, Naimans and Merkits. They stole each other's animals and wives, and revenge for a killing could last through three generations.

They believed that a great power lived in the Eternal Blue Sky, and they prayed to it before every important task. To the south lay China, a rich land with great cities, and it watched the tribes with worry.
A boy named Temujin was born near the Onon River in about 1162, although historians are not sure of the exact year. His father, Yesugei, was a minor clan leader who had many enemies.

Temujin grew up with his mother, Hoelun, and with younger brothers called Khasar, Khachiun and Temuge, and a little sister, Temulun. Hoelun was strong and clever, and she had once been carried off by Yesugei from another man's wedding.

When Temujin was about nine, Yesugei took him to the Onggirat people, his mother's tribe, to find him a wife. They stayed with Dei Sechen, whose daughter Borte was a year older, and Temujin was left there as the custom demanded.

On the road Yesugei met some Tatars, the old enemies of his clan, and they invited him to share their meal. He soon felt ill and sent for Temujin, but when the boy rode home, his father had already died.

The leaders of the clan decided that a widow with small children was not worth protecting. They packed up their tents, took the animals and rode away, leaving Hoelun and her children with almost nothing.
For several hard years Hoelun fed her children on wild roots, berries and the small fish that her sons could catch. They owned only a few horses, and they were always afraid of raiders.

Hunger and pride caused terrible quarrels among the boys. When Temujin and his brother Khasar felt that their older half-brother Begter was stealing their food, they killed him, and Hoelun was furious.
As Temujin grew taller, the Tayichiud began to see him as a danger and sent men to capture him. They made him wear a heavy wooden collar, and they moved him from tent to tent.

One night, while the guards were busy at a feast, Temujin hit one of them with his heavy collar and ran to the river. He lay in the water with only his face showing, and the moon lit the whole valley.
Soon afterwards thieves stole almost all of the family's horses, and Temujin rode after them alone. A young man named Bo'orchu offered to help him, and the two friends brought the horses home.
When he was about sixteen, Temujin rode back to the Onggirat to claim his promised wife. Borte's family had kept their word, and the young couple were married.
Borte's mother had given the couple a splendid coat of black sable fur as a wedding gift. Temujin took it to Toghrul, the powerful ruler of the Kereit, who had once been his father's sworn brother.
Not long afterwards, riders from the Merkit tribe attacked the camp at dawn. They took Borte as a prize, and they said it was revenge for the woman Yesugei had taken from them long before.

Temujin had escaped by hiding on Burkhan Khaldun, a forested mountain that the Mongols considered sacred. When the danger had passed, he faced the sun and promised to honour the mountain for the rest of his life.
Temujin could not rescue his wife alone, so he rode to Toghrul and asked for an army. Toghrul agreed, and he told Temujin to send a message to his old friend Jamukha too.
The three armies crossed the river by night and attacked the Merkit camp before anyone could wake. In the confusion Temujin rode shouting for his wife, and Borte heard him and ran into his arms.
Borte gave birth to a son soon after the rescue, and he was named Jochi. Nobody could be sure who the father was, but Temujin accepted the boy and raised him as his own.

Jamukha and Temujin had sworn an oath of brotherhood when they were boys, giving each other gifts such as knucklebones and arrows. A sworn brother, called an anda, was as close to a person as a real brother.
One day Jamukha said something that Temujin did not understand, and Temujin went to ask his mother and his wife. They advised him to leave Jamukha, and he took his people away in the night.
Many of the people who had been in Jamukha's camp chose to follow Temujin. Their friendship was over, and the two men would now become rivals.
In about 1189, a group of Mongol nobles met and chose Temujin as their khan, or ruler. They swore to obey him in war, and they promised to give him the best of their spoils.
Jamukha was angry and gathered a large army to attack his old friend. In the battle of Dalan Baljut, Temujin lost and had to retreat, although the exact date is uncertain.

Unlike most steppe rulers, Temujin chose his helpers for their talent and loyalty, not for their noble families. Men who had once been servants or herders became his commanders and his closest friends.
In 1196 the Jin rulers of northern China asked Temujin and Toghrul to help them defeat the Tatars. The allies won, and the Jin gave both leaders grand titles in return.
Temujin made an important rule that nobody could take any spoils until the battle had been won. Afterwards everything was shared out fairly, even with the families of men who had died.
Toghrul's son was jealous of Temujin, and he persuaded his father to turn against his old ally. In 1203 the Kereit army defeated Temujin in a hard battle, and he was wounded.
Temujin retreated to a muddy lake at Baljuna with only a handful of men, perhaps about nineteen. Tradition says they drank the dirty water together and swore to share good and bad times.
Temujin rebuilt his small army in secret and attacked the Kereit camp by surprise. They fought for three days, and in the end the Kereit surrendered.
The next year, Temujin turned against the Naimans, who ruled the lands to the west. Jamukha joined their side, but the Naiman army was defeated and its ruler was killed.
Jamukha was finally betrayed by his own men, who handed him over to Temujin. Temujin punished the traitors, because he believed that nobody should betray their leader.
In 1206, leaders from all the tribes met at a great assembly called a kuriltai. They raised a banner of nine white horsetails and gave Temujin the title Genghis Khan.
Scholars are not sure what Genghis meant, but it probably suggested a strong and fair ruler. Temujin was now about forty-four years old, and he had spent most of his life in struggle.
Genghis Khan organised his army into groups of ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand men. He mixed men from different tribes, so that their loyalty was to their unit and their leader.
After the assembly, Genghis Khan rewarded the men who had helped him in the hard years. The Secret History lists about ninety-five commanders, each in charge of a thousand families.

He built a bodyguard of ten thousand men, called the keshig, to protect him day and night. Many of the guards were the sons of commanders, and the keshig also trained the future leaders of the empire.
A set of laws, later called the Yassa, was said to apply to everyone, including the khan's family. It banned crimes such as stealing animals and kidnapping women, which had caused many wars.
Genghis Khan appointed Shigi Khutukhu, an adopted brother, as his chief judge. His job was to record all decisions in writing, so that they would not be forgotten or changed.
The Mongols had never written their language down until they captured a Naiman official named Tata-tonga, who could write the Uyghur script. Genghis Khan told him to teach his sons to read and write.
The Mongols followed the old religion of the sky, but Genghis Khan was curious about all faiths. He freed priests, monks and teachers from taxes and asked them to pray for him.
Genghis Khan and Borte had four sons, named Jochi, Chagatai, Ogedei and Tolui. They were very different in character, and their rivalries would shape the future of the empire.
The heart of the Mongol army was the mounted archer, who carried a short but powerful bow. It was made of wood, horn and animal sinew glued together, and it could shoot far and with great force.

A good archer could even turn around in the saddle and shoot backwards. Riders are said to have released their arrows while all four hooves were off the ground, so that the movement did not spoil the aim.
Mongol riders used stirrups and strong saddles that let them stand up and aim. Their armies could cover many kilometres in a day, far more than the slow armies of Europe and China.
Each soldier usually had several horses, and he switched from one to another during the day. This allowed the army to keep moving fast without tiring out its animals.
A soldier needed very little baggage, because he carried dried meat, dried milk curd and a water bag. Travellers reported that in an emergency a rider could even drink a little blood from his horse.
Before a battle, Mongol scouts and spies learned as much as they could about the enemy's army, land and cities. During the fight, flags, drums and arrows with whistles sent signals to every unit.

One of their favourite tricks was the false retreat, in which a small group of riders pretended to run away. The enemy charged after them in disorder, and then hidden Mongol units attacked from the sides.

Every winter the army held a great hunt, in which thousands of riders formed a huge ring and slowly closed it. The animals inside were driven toward the centre, and the exercise taught the soldiers to move together.
Discipline in the Mongol army was strict, and orders had to be obeyed without delay. Travellers reported that if one man ran away, the rest of his group could be punished too.
When the army reached a city, it usually offered the people a chance to surrender. Those who gave in were often spared, but those who fought might be destroyed.
In 1205 the Mongols began to raid Western Xia, a kingdom in the north-west of China. The raiders were good at fighting in open country, but they had never before faced strong city walls.
In 1209 the Mongols besieged the Xia capital and tried to flood it by breaking a river bank. The water also flooded their camp, but the Xia king still decided to submit and pay tribute.

In the same years the Uyghurs, a people of oasis towns and trade routes, chose to join the Mongols peacefully. Their ruler became like a fifth son to Genghis Khan, and Uyghur scribes became useful officials.

Engineers and craftsmen from the conquered lands joined the Mongol army and taught it how to attack walls. Together they built catapults, ladders and battering rams, and later even weapons that used gunpowder.

The Jin court demanded that Genghis Khan bow to its new emperor, but he refused and, the old story says, spat on the ground. In 1211 the Mongols invaded and won a great victory at a place called Yehuling.
In 1213 the Mongols forced their way through a narrow mountain pass into the great plain of northern China. They ravaged the countryside, and the Jin capital agreed to pay them a heavy tribute.

Soon afterwards the Jin emperor moved his court south to the city of Kaifeng, which Genghis Khan took as a sign of distrust. The Mongols returned, and the old capital, Zhongdu, fell in 1215 after a long siege.

One of the people found in the ruined capital was Yelu Chucai, a Khitan scholar who knew the stars, languages and law. He joined Genghis Khan, and over the years he taught the Mongols how a government could work.
In 1217 Genghis Khan went back to Mongolia and left his able general Muqali in command in China. With only a small army, Muqali kept winning cities and holding the lands that the Mongols had taken.

Kuchlug, a Naiman prince, had taken over the western kingdom of Qara Khitai, and he treated its Muslim people harshly. In 1218 the general Jebe defeated him and announced that everyone could follow their own religion.

To the west of the Mongols lay the empire of Khwarazm, ruled by Shah Muhammad from great cities such as Samarkand. Genghis Khan proposed a treaty of friendship and trade, because he knew that the caravans of the Silk Road were valuable.
In 1218 a caravan of traders sent by the Mongols reached the border city of Otrar. The governor, Inalchuq, accused the traders of being spies, killed them and kept their goods.
Genghis Khan sent envoys to demand that the governor be handed over for punishment. The shah refused, killed one of the envoys and had the beards of the others cut off, which was a great insult.

Genghis Khan is said to have climbed a mountain alone and prayed to the Eternal Blue Sky for three days. Then he gathered his army, which may have numbered up to about one hundred thousand men, though estimates differ.

Genghis Khan split his army into several columns, which approached the enemy cities from different directions. One column, led by Jochi, rode down a river, while two of his other sons attacked the border city of Otrar.
In February 1220 the Mongols reached Bukhara, a famous centre of learning. The townspeople opened the gates, but the soldiers in the citadel kept fighting, and a fire spread through the wooden city.

In March 1220 the army reached Samarkand, the shah's capital, which had strong walls and a large garrison. After only a few days the city surrendered, and the soldiers who had defended it were executed.
Shah Muhammad fled from city to city with the Mongol generals Jebe and Subutai close behind. At last he died, sick and almost alone, on a small island in the Caspian Sea.
At the siege of Urgench in 1221, Jochi and Chagatai quarrelled so badly that the attack was delayed. Genghis Khan told Ogedei to take command, and the city finally fell with terrible destruction.
In 1221 the cities of Merv and Nishapur were attacked and badly destroyed. Medieval writers gave huge numbers for the dead, but modern historians think these figures were too high.

Jalal ad-Din, the shah's brave son, defeated a Mongol force at Parwan in 1221, a rare setback for the Mongols. Genghis Khan chased him to the Indus River, where the prince jumped his horse into the water and escaped.

Genghis Khan heard about a Daoist master named Changchun, who was said to be wise and very old. He invited the monk to visit, and the old man travelled for about two years across mountains and deserts.

Genghis Khan hoped that the monk might know a secret medicine for a long life. Changchun told him honestly that there was no such medicine, and the khan respected his honesty and freed Daoist monks from taxes.

After the shah died, Jebe and Subutai did not go home, but rode on with about twenty thousand men to explore the west. They had permission to learn about those lands and to fight any army that opposed them.

To cross the high Caucasus mountains, the Mongols persuaded the guides of a walled port to show them a pass. On the far side they met the Alans and the Cumans, who were allies, and the Mongols found a way to separate them.

The Cumans fled to the lands of the Rus, whose princes agreed that they should work together against the new danger. The Mongols sent envoys to say that they had no quarrel with the Rus, but the Rus killed them.
The Mongols retreated for about nine days, and the Rus armies followed them in disorder, eager to win. In May 1223, by the Kalka River, the Mongols turned and destroyed them.
After the victory at Kalka, the generals turned east and crossed the steppe, fighting the Bulgars on the way. They rode for thousands of kilometres before they rejoined Genghis Khan.

Genghis Khan began his journey home in 1223, leaving governors in the conquered cities. His eldest son, Jochi, who had refused to speak with him, died a few years later, though the exact date is uncertain.
Genghis Khan knew that the empire needed a clear plan for the future. He chose Ogedei, his third son, as his heir, partly because Jochi and Chagatai could not agree.
Western Xia had refused to send soldiers for the war against Khwarazm and had mocked the khan. In 1226 Genghis Khan marched against it, and the Mongol army destroyed several of its cities.
During the campaign, Genghis Khan fell from his horse while hunting wild horses and became ill with a fever. His advisers urged him to go home, but he refused to turn back.

Genghis Khan died in August 1227 at about sixty-five years old, while his army was still fighting in Western Xia. Historians do not agree on the cause, which may have been illness, an injury or a wound.
His body was carried back to Mongolia, and the grave was hidden so that nobody could disturb it. Legends say that the riders killed everyone they met on the road, though this may only be a story.
Tolui, the youngest son, looked after the empire for two years as regent, until a new khan could be chosen. According to Mongol custom, the youngest son inherited the family's homeland.
In 1229 a great assembly was held, and the princes chose Ogedei as the second great khan. He was about forty-three years old, and he was generous and friendly.
Ogedei decided to finish the war against the Jin, and he made an alliance with the Chinese Song dynasty in the south. In 1234 the Jin were destroyed, and their last emperor took his own life.
Around 1235 Ogedei built the capital of the empire at Karakorum, in the middle of Mongolia. Craftsmen from many countries came to build walls and a palace on the grassy plain.
Some Mongol nobles wanted to turn the farmland of northern China into pasture for horses. Yelu Chucai persuaded Ogedei that it would be better to tax the farmers, and a census was ordered.
At another great assembly in 1235, the Mongol leaders decided on a series of new campaigns. They planned to attack the Song in China, to push into Korea, and to send a great army to the west.
In 1236 a huge Mongol army set out to the west under Batu, a grandson of Genghis Khan. The planning was done by the old general Subutai, who had already seen the Rus and their rivers.
The Mongols first attacked the Volga Bulgars, whose rich trading cities stood on the great river. They also defeated the Cumans on the grassland, and the survivors fled in every direction.

The land of the Rus was divided among many princes who were often at odds with one another. In the winter of 1237 the Mongols attacked, riding over frozen rivers that served as roads through the forest.
The Mongols first demanded a tenth of everything from the city of Ryazan, and its prince refused. After a siege of about five days, in December 1237, the city was captured and burned.
Early in 1238 the Mongols took the town of Kolomna and then a small wooden fortress called Moscow. It was still unimportant at that time, but it would grow into a famous city.
The Grand Prince, Yuri, left his capital Vladimir to gather soldiers in the north. In February 1238 the Mongols attacked the city, broke through its walls and burned it.
A few weeks later, the Mongols found Yuri's army by the Sit River and surrounded it. They won the battle easily, and Yuri himself was killed.
A small town named Kozelsk resisted the Mongols for about seven weeks, and many of the attackers died. Soon after that, the army turned back before the spring thaw turned the land to mud.
After resting on the steppe for more than a year, the Mongols came back and took one city after another in the south. The great city of Kyiv, with its golden domes, fell to them in December 1240.

After the conquest, the Rus princes had to travel to the Mongol court and pay tribute to the khan. This arrangement lasted for more than two hundred years, though historians disagree about how heavy the burden really was.
Thousands of Cumans, who had fled from the Mongols, were given shelter by King Bela IV of Hungary. The Mongols saw this as an insult, and they demanded that the king hand the refugees back.
In the early months of 1241 the Mongols divided their army into several groups. One went north into Poland, and the main force crossed the Carpathian mountains into Hungary.
In Poland the Mongols raided and burned the towns of Sandomierz and Krakow. Many Polish princes and nobles fled to the mountains or abroad rather than face them.

On 9 April 1241, near the town of Legnica, Duke Henry's army met the Mongols before the king of Bohemia could arrive. The Mongols pretended to retreat, drew the knights out of formation, and then destroyed them.
