Two days later, on 11 April, the Mongols reached the Sajo River, where the Hungarian army had made a camp. They crossed the river early in the morning and attacked the camp from all sides.
King Bela escaped from the battle and fled across the country until he reached the Adriatic coast. The Mongols burned the town of Pest and spent the summer and winter raiding the land.
In December 1241, the great khan Ogedei died in Karakorum after a long feast. When the news came, the Mongol princes in Europe had to think about the choice of a new khan.
In 1242 the Mongol armies turned around and rode back to the east, leaving Europe. Historians still argue about the reasons, but the death of Ogedei was probably the most important one.
Batu did not go home to Karakorum but made his own capital, Sarai, on the Volga River. His realm, which later became known as the Golden Horde, ruled the Russian lands for generations.
Europeans were shocked by the raid and by the Mongol way of war. In 1245 Pope Innocent IV sent a monk named John of Plano Carpini to discover who these strangers really were.
After Ogedei died, his widow, Toregene, took charge of the empire as regent. For about five years she made the decisions, and she replaced many of her husband's advisers with her own.

Mongol women were far less restricted than women in many other societies of that time. They managed the herds and the camp when the men were away, and queens commanded their own households and advisers.

In 1246 an enormous assembly was held, with thousands of guests from distant countries, and Guyuk was chosen as great khan. The monk John of Plano Carpini, who had travelled from Europe, was there to see it.
Guyuk was already ill when he became khan, and he died in 1248 after ruling for only two years. He was probably marching west to settle his differences with his cousin Batu.

Sorghaghtani Beki was the widow of Genghis Khan's youngest son, Tolui, and she was a Christian from the Kereit people. She raised four remarkable sons, called Mongke, Khubilai, Hulegu and Ariq Boke, and she was respected for her wisdom.
With the support of Batu and of his mother, Mongke was elected as great khan in 1251. He then ordered many of his rivals from the family of Ogedei to be tried and executed.
Mongke was a serious and hard-working ruler who disliked waste. He ordered a census of the empire, set regular taxes and tried to stop officials from taking more than they should.

In 1254 a friar named William of Rubruck, who had been sent by the king of France, finally reached Karakorum. He described a capital that was smaller than he had expected, but full of people from many lands.

At the entrance of the palace stood a large silver tree that had been made by a French goldsmith named Guillaume Boucher. Pipes in its branches poured out different drinks, such as wine and mare's milk, into silver bowls.

In May 1254, Mongke invited Christians, Muslims and Buddhists to debate their beliefs at his court. Afterwards, according to Rubruck, he said that God had given the hand many fingers, and men many paths.

Mongke planned two great campaigns for the 1250s, which he hoped would complete his grandfather's work. One was against the Song dynasty of southern China, and the other was in western Asia, under his younger brother Hulegu.

In Persia a religious group called the Ismailis held mountain fortresses, including a famous castle called Alamut. In 1256 Hulegu's army forced their leader to surrender, and the castles were destroyed.

Hulegu sent a message to the caliph in Baghdad, who was the spiritual leader of the Muslim world, telling him to submit. The caliph, whose family had ruled for five hundred years, refused to believe that anyone could attack his city.
In January 1258 several Mongol columns closed in on Baghdad from different sides. They built a wall around the city, brought up catapults and bombarded the walls for about two weeks.
The Mongols entered Baghdad and sacked it for about a week. The caliph was executed, and many thousands of people were killed, though historians disagree about how many.

Hulegu's wife, Doquz Khatun, was a Christian, and she asked that Christians in Baghdad should be spared. Many libraries were damaged, and a famous story says the Tigris ran black with ink, though this may be exaggerated.
In 1260 the Mongol army marched into Syria, helped by Christian allies from Armenia and Georgia. Aleppo was captured after a short siege, and the citizens of Damascus surrendered peacefully.
In August 1259 Mongke died during the war against the Song in China, probably of illness. Hulegu took most of his army back toward Persia, leaving only a small force in Syria.

On 3 September 1260 the Mamluk army of Egypt, led by Sultan Qutuz and the commander Baibars, met a small Mongol force at Ain Jalut. The Mamluks used the Mongol trick of a false retreat, and they won the battle.

The Mongols never succeeded in conquering Egypt, and the Mamluks held their border for many years. Hulegu wanted revenge, but he was soon drawn into a war with his cousin Berke, the Muslim ruler of the Golden Horde.

Khubilai was born in 1215, and as a young man he became very curious about China. He gathered Chinese scholars, Buddhist monks and a Tibetan teacher named Pagpa around him, and he listened to their advice.
In 1260, after Mongke died, two of his brothers each held an assembly of supporters. Khubilai was declared khan in northern China, and Ariq Boke was declared khan at Karakorum.
The two brothers fought a civil war that lasted until 1264. Khubilai controlled the wealthy lands of China, which gave him food and supplies, and he finally forced Ariq Boke to surrender.
In 1267 Khubilai began to build a grand new capital, called Khanbaliq, on the site of modern Beijing. It was laid out with straight, wide streets, great walls and a vast palace.

In 1271 Khubilai gave his government in China the dynastic name Yuan, a word from an old Chinese book of wisdom. He now claimed to rule China as an emperor, in the Chinese tradition, as well as ruling as a khan.

The Yuan government divided people into groups, with the Mongols at the top and the people of southern China at the bottom. Many Chinese scholars lost their old posts, although some of them held office under Khubilai.

The Mongols besieged the Song city of Xiangyang for about five years, from 1268 to 1273. Persian engineers built powerful new catapults, and the city finally surrendered after its defences were broken.
In 1276 the great Song capital of Lin'an, now Hangzhou, surrendered to the Mongol general Bayan. The young Song emperor and the empress dowager handed over their seal, and the city was spared.
A small Song court kept fighting from ships off the south coast until 1279. At the battle of Yamen the Song fleet was destroyed, and all of China came under Mongol rule.
To feed his huge capital, Khubilai improved the roads and extended the Grand Canal. The engineer Guo Shoujing helped to build a canal that carried grain and goods from the south to Beijing.

By the late thirteenth century a traveller could cross all of Asia, from China to the Black Sea, in lands ruled by Mongols. Later historians called this period the Mongol Peace, although the empire was often at war with itself.
The Mongols built a network of relay stations, called the yam, along their main roads. Each station kept fresh horses and food, and a messenger could change horses and keep riding without a pause.
Officials and envoys carried a small metal tablet called a paiza, which worked rather like a passport. It gave the holder the right to food, fresh horses and a place to sleep at every station.
The Mongol rulers wanted the roads to be safe for trade, so they punished bandits severely. Officials in a district could be held responsible for any theft that took place there.

Caravans carried silk, spices, silver, porcelain and horses across Asia, and the markets of the great cities were full of goods from distant lands. Along the roads, inns for travellers and their animals grew up at regular distances.

The Yuan government printed paper money with a red seal, and people were required to accept it in place of coins. Visitors from other countries were astonished, but when too many notes were printed, the money lost its value.
In 1271 a young Venetian named Marco Polo left home with his father and his uncle, who were both merchants. After a journey of about three and a half years, they reached the court of Khubilai Khan.

Marco Polo spent about seventeen years in the service of the khan, travelling widely. In 1291 he left China by sea with a Mongol princess, who was going to marry the ruler of Persia, and he reached Venice in 1295.
Marco Polo was later captured in a war, and in a Genoese prison he told his story to the writer Rustichello. The book became famous, although some scholars doubt parts of it.
Rabban Sauma was a Christian monk who had been born near Khanbaliq. In 1287 the Mongol ruler of Persia sent him to Europe, where he met the kings of France and England.
The Mongol rulers valued skilled people, and they brought scholars, doctors and craftsmen from many countries to work at their courts. They often did not care where a clever person had been born.

In 1259 Hulegu founded an observatory at Maragha, in Persia, and put the great scholar Nasir al-Din Tusi in charge. Astronomers from several countries worked there, and they made new tables of the movements of the planets.

Khubilai invited a Persian astronomer to Khanbaliq, and he also employed the Chinese scientist Guo Shoujing. In 1281 they produced a calendar that measured the year at 365 days, 5 hours and 49 minutes, which is very accurate.

Doctors from Persia and China exchanged knowledge, and some of their books were translated. The Persian doctor and minister Rashid al-Din arranged for Chinese medical texts, including ones about taking the pulse, to be translated into Persian.

Around 1300 the Persian minister Rashid al-Din was asked to write a history of the Mongols. It grew into the first history of the whole known world, and experts from China, India and Europe helped him.
Chinese potters began to decorate white porcelain with a blue colour that came from Persian cobalt. The new blue-and-white porcelain was loved in the Middle East, and it was soon traded across Asia.
In 1294 the Mongol ruler of Persia tried to introduce paper money, copying the Chinese system. People refused to trust the paper, the markets closed, and the plan was dropped within a few weeks.
In China the Mongols met gunpowder weapons, such as bombs and rockets, and they used them in their sieges. Historians think that knowledge of gunpowder spread westward along with the Mongol armies.

Khubilai wanted one script that could write all the languages of his empire. In 1269 the Tibetan monk Pagpa designed a new alphabet, but it was used mainly on official documents and never became widely popular.
In 1330 a court official named Hu Sihui wrote a book about food and health for the Yuan court. It included recipes with spices and dishes from Mongolia, China, Persia and other places.
In 1274 Khubilai sent a fleet of ships from Korea to attack Japan. The Mongols landed at Hakata Bay and fought the samurai, but then they sailed away after a night of storms.
The Japanese expected the Mongols to return, so they built a long stone wall around Hakata Bay. When Khubilai sent envoys to demand surrender, the Japanese rulers had them executed.
In 1281 two huge fleets, which carried more than a hundred thousand men according to many accounts, set out for Japan. In August a typhoon wrecked many of the ships, and the attack failed.

In Vietnam the Tran dynasty fought off the Mongols three times, in 1258, 1285 and 1287 to 1288. In the last war, the general Tran Hung Dao hid iron-tipped stakes in the Bach Dang River and trapped the Mongol ships.

In 1293 Khubilai sent a fleet to Java to punish a king who had insulted his envoy. The Mongols were drawn into a local quarrel, and a clever prince named Raden Wijaya turned on them and drove them out.
In hot and wet forests the Mongol cavalry lost much of its power, because horses became sick and could not move fast. Wherever the grass ended, the old advantages of the Mongols faded.
Khubilai had suffered many personal sorrows, including the deaths of his favourite wife and his chosen heir. He died in 1294, aged about seventy-eight, after more than thirty years as great khan.

By the time Khubilai died, the empire had divided into four main khanates, each ruled by a different branch of the family. They were the Yuan in China, the Golden Horde in Russia, the Ilkhanate in Persia and the Chagatai in Central Asia.

In the western khanates, many Mongol rulers chose the religion of their subjects. Berke of the Golden Horde and Ghazan of Persia both became Muslims, and Ozbeg Khan made Islam the official religion of his lands in 1313.
As the generations passed, the Mongol rulers in each land adopted the language and customs of their subjects. The Yuan became more Chinese, the Ilkhans more Persian and the Golden Horde more Turkic.

After Khubilai, the Yuan emperors often quarrelled over the throne, and many of them reigned for only a few years. Too much paper money lost its value, and in the 1340s the Yellow River flooded and caused famine.
In 1351 groups of rebels called the Red Turbans rose against the Yuan, and soon the revolt spread across much of China. One of their leaders, Zhu Yuanzhang, was an orphan who had once been a monk.
In 1368 Zhu Yuanzhang proclaimed the new Ming dynasty, and his army marched on Khanbaliq. The last Yuan emperor fled to the north with his court, and Mongol rule in China was over.

A terrible illness, later called the Black Death, appeared in the 1330s, and it probably began in Central Asia. In 2022 scientists studied graves near Lake Issyk-Kul from 1338 and 1339 and found signs of the plague.

In 1346 an army of the Golden Horde besieged Caffa, a port on the Black Sea that belonged to traders from Genoa. Plague broke out among the besiegers, and an old account says they threw bodies over the walls.
In 1347 the sickness reached Sicily and soon spread through the ports of Italy, then through all of Europe. It killed perhaps a third or more of the people, though the numbers are uncertain.
The Mongol states in the west were falling apart. The Ilkhanate in Persia had collapsed in 1335, when its ruler died without an heir, and the Chagatai khanate split in two.
Timur was a Turkic conqueror who rose to power in Central Asia in the 1370s. He was not descended from Genghis Khan, so he ruled in the name of a Mongol prince and tried to copy his heroes.

Under Timur's blows the Golden Horde broke up into smaller khanates, while Moscow became stronger. In 1480 Ivan III refused to pay tribute, and the two armies faced each other on the Ugra River until the khan withdrew.
In 1526 a prince named Babur, who was descended from both Timur and Genghis Khan, defeated the sultan of Delhi. He founded the Mughal empire, which ruled most of India for about three hundred years.
The Mongol conquests killed very many people, and whole cities were destroyed. Medieval writers gave huge numbers, but modern historians disagree widely about the real figures.
In parts of Persia and Central Asia, the water channels that made farming possible were wrecked. When the farmers were killed or fled, the land often took generations to recover.

At the same time, the Mongol empire connected peoples who had known little about each other. Marco Polo's book was read by many people, and it was among the books that Columbus owned and wrote notes in.

The Secret History of the Mongols was written in the thirteenth century, and it is the oldest Mongol account of the life of Genghis Khan. It does not hide his faults, and it tells of killings, quarrels and mistakes.

In 2003 a team of scientists reported a male genetic line carried by about eight in every hundred men across a huge part of Asia. It began in Mongolia about a thousand years ago, and it may belong to Genghis Khan's family.
In the twentieth century Mongolia became a communist state, close to the Soviet Union. It discouraged praise for Genghis Khan, but after the peaceful revolution of 1990 he returned to honour.
Today a huge steel statue of Genghis Khan on his horse, about forty metres high, stands on a hill east of Ulaanbaatar. The new international airport of Mongolia also carries his name.

Many families in Mongolia still live in gers and move with their animals through the seasons, much as their ancestors did. Each July the national festival of Naadam brings wrestling, archery and horse racing.
In the lands that were attacked, such as Iran, Iraq, Russia and Ukraine, people remember the conquests as a time of fear. Many old cities still carry the scars of those years.

The story of the Mongol empire holds two truths at once, a world that was connected and a world that was wounded. Mongolia honours Genghis Khan as the father of the nation, while others remember only the pain.
C1C2: Across the middle of Asia, from the borders of China almost to the edge of Europe, there runs a great belt of grassland that people call the steppe. Few trees interrupt it, the winters are fierce, and the summers are short and dry, so farming is hard in most places. Yet this harsh and open country was the cradle of the largest land empire the world has ever seen.

The climate of the steppe is a land of extremes, with winters so bitter that a herder's breath freezes on his scarf and summers hot enough to scorch the pastures. Rain is scarce and unreliable, and a single dry season could decide whether a family's animals lived or died. People who survived there learned to read the weather, the grass and the sky as other peoples read books.

A traditional Mongol family kept five kinds of animals, which were horses, sheep, goats, cattle and camels, and each kind was valued for something different. The sheep and goats gave meat and wool, the cattle pulled carts, and the camels carried the heaviest loads across the desert to the south. Wealth on the steppe was not measured in gold or in land but in the size and health of the herd.

The Mongols lived in round tents that are called gers today, each one built from a lattice of wooden poles and covered with thick layers of felt pressed from sheep's wool. A family could take its tent down in an hour or so, pack it onto a cart or a camel, and set it up again wherever the grass was better. The doorway usually faced south, away from the worst of the winter wind, and the hearth in the centre was the heart of the household.

Grain was scarce on the steppe, so the Mongols lived mostly on what their animals gave them, which meant boiled meat, fresh milk, yoghurt and cheese dried until it was as hard as stone. Mare's milk was fermented in leather bags until it became a slightly sour and slightly alcoholic drink, a favourite at every feast. Food of this kind was light, nourishing and easy to carry, and that would matter very much in the years to come.

A herd that stayed in one place would soon strip the grass bare, so the herders followed the seasons in a pattern that their families had known for generations. They sheltered through the bitter winters in protected valleys and river bends, then spread out across the open plains when the summer grass came up green and tall. Moving was not a hardship to them but a normal and well-organised part of life, and it made them very hard people to catch.

Mongol children were put on horses when they were barely old enough to walk, and the youngest were sometimes tied to the saddle until their balance improved. By the time they were teenagers, they could ride for hours across rough country, herd animals alone, and shoot a bow with real skill. For most of them the horse was not a tool but an extension of the body, as natural to use as a hand.

The Mongol horse was a small, shaggy and rather ugly animal, much shorter than the great war horses of Europe, but it was extraordinarily tough. In the depths of winter it could dig through snow with its hooves to reach the dry grass beneath, so that it needed no stable and no grain. Such an animal could carry a rider for days on end across country where a pampered horse would quickly have starved.

There was no Mongol nation in the twelfth century, only a patchwork of tribes and clans, among them the Mongols, the Tatars, the Kereit, the Naimans and the Merkits, which shared a way of life but not a ruler. Raiding was common, for animals and for wives, and a killing created a debt of blood that a son was expected to repay and a grandson to remember. Without a strong leader to bind them, the tribes wasted most of their strength fighting one another.

The Mongols worshipped the Eternal Blue Sky, which they called Tengri, and believed that it watched over their lives and gave power to rulers it favoured. To the south, beyond the Gobi desert, lay the rich farmland and walled cities of northern China, where the Jin dynasty watched the restless tribes with a mixture of fear and contempt. Into this divided world a boy was about to be born who would unite the tribes and turn the whole picture upside down.

Temujin, the boy who would become Genghis Khan, was born in about 1162 near the Onon River, although the exact year is disputed because nobody on the steppe kept written records of such things. His father, Yesugei, led a small clan and had earned both a reputation for courage and a long list of enemies. Much of what we know about his childhood comes from the Secret History of the Mongols, a book written down after his death, which mixes sober fact with legend.

Temujin grew up in a lively household that included his mother, Hoelun, three younger brothers named Khasar, Khachiun and Temuge, and a baby sister called Temulun. Hoelun was a proud and capable woman who, the stories say, had been seized by Yesugei on her wedding journey from a Merkit bridegroom, which was how marriages sometimes began on the steppe. She would prove to be the most important teacher of her eldest son's life.

When Temujin was about nine years old, his father took him toward the lands of the Onggirat, his mother's people, to find a bride among their daughters. They met a man named Dei Sechen, who spoke warmly of a dream about a white falcon and offered his own daughter, Borte, a girl a year older than Temujin. By custom the boy stayed behind to live with his bride's family, so Yesugei left a horse as a pledge, said farewell and rode home alone.

On the road home Yesugei came upon a camp of Tatars, the traditional enemies of his people, who invited him to share their meal, and the rules of hospitality meant that he could hardly refuse. Within days he was gravely ill, and the old account says that the Tatars had put poison in his food in revenge for earlier wrongs. Temujin rode home as fast as his horse would carry him, only to find his father dead and the camp full of mourning, while the clan began to ask what use a boy and a widow could be.

The leaders of Yesugei's clan, the Tayichiud, decided that a widow with a handful of small children was not worth protecting, and they packed up their tents and drove their herds away. Hoelun, who is said to have seized a banner and ridden after them to shame them, persuaded a few to turn back, but even those soon drifted off. The family was left on the empty steppe with almost nothing, an easy target for any enemy who cared to take advantage.

For several hard years Hoelun kept her children alive on wild onions and roots, on berries that she gathered from the riverbanks, and on the small fish that her sons learned to catch with hooks they made from bent needles. The family owned only a few horses and a handful of other animals, and they lived in constant fear that raiders would find them. Hardship of this sort, the storytellers insisted, taught the young Temujin that loyalty was precious and that a leader who could not protect his people had no right to lead them.

Hunger and pride led to bitter quarrels among the boys, and the Secret History does not hide that the family itself was sometimes violent. When Temujin and his brother Khasar felt that their older half-brother Begter was claiming food and authority that he had no right to, the two of them shot him dead, and Hoelun scolded them furiously for destroying their own family. Even in his teens Temujin was willing to act ruthlessly against anyone who stood in his way, even a member of his own household.

As Temujin grew tall and strong, the Tayichiud leader Targutai began to fear that the boy might one day try to take revenge, and he sent a band of men to seize him. The captive was made to wear a heavy wooden collar, a portable prison that locked his hands and head together, and he was passed from tent to tent so that every family took a turn guarding him. It was a humiliating punishment for a boy whose father had once been their leader.

One summer night, while the whole camp was busy with a feast, Temujin struck his guard with the heavy collar, ran to the river and lay down in the shallows with only his face above the water. The moon was bright, and a man named Sorqan Shira, who was searching with the others, saw him there but quietly told the searchers that the boy was nowhere to be found. Later his family cut off the collar and hid Temujin in a cart of wool until the danger had passed, a debt of kindness that he never forgot.

Soon afterwards thieves stole nearly all of the family's horses, and Temujin set out alone to follow their tracks across the plain. He met a young man named Bo'orchu, who offered a fresh horse and rode beside him without asking for any reward, and together the two of them recovered the herd. Bo'orchu became his first true companion, the earliest of the loyal followers who would one day help him to rule half the world.

When he was about sixteen, Temujin rode back to the lands of the Onggirat to claim the bride who had been promised to him years before. Her father, Dei Sechen, had kept his word, though he might easily have chosen a richer son-in-law, and the wedding took place with the customary feasting. Borte was a calm, intelligent young woman, and she would remain his closest adviser for the rest of her life.

As part of her dowry, Borte brought a magnificent coat of black sable fur, which was a gift fit for a great ruler. Rather than keep it, he carried it to Toghrul, the powerful ruler of the Kereit people, who had been his father's sworn brother, and presented it to him as a gift. In return he asked Toghrul to treat him as a son, and the older man agreed to protect him and to help him gather the people who had deserted his father.

Not long afterwards, a band of Merkit warriors attacked Temujin's camp at dawn, in revenge for the wife that Yesugei had once taken from their tribe. The family scattered in panic, Temujin and his brothers escaped on horseback into the forested mountains, and Borte, who could not flee in time, was captured and given to a Merkit man as his wife. It was a catastrophe for a young leader who had very few followers and no army of his own.

Temujin had saved himself by hiding for three days on Burkhan Khaldun, a forested mountain that the Mongols considered sacred and that protected him from his pursuers. When the danger had passed, he came down, turned toward the rising sun, offered a libation of milk and swore that he and his descendants would honour the mountain for ever. Throughout his life he kept this feeling of gratitude toward the sky and the sacred places of his homeland, and it was later said that he would be buried near the mountain.

Temujin knew that he could not rescue his wife with his few followers, so he went to Toghrul and begged for the help of the Kereit army. Toghrul agreed at once and sent him to find Jamukha, the boyhood friend who had since become the leader of a clan of his own and who commanded several thousand riders. Jamukha promised to join them, and the three leaders agreed on a plan to ride against the Merkits together.

The three armies crossed a wide river by night and struck the Merkit camp so suddenly that the warriors had no time to form a defence, and the Merkits scattered in terror. In the darkness and confusion, Temujin rode among the fleeing people, shouting his wife's name, and Borte recognised his voice, tore herself from the crowd and ran toward his horse. He leapt down and caught her in his arms, and the old story says that the two of them held each other tightly, for he had gone to war for the sake of one person.

Only a short time after her return, Borte gave birth to a son whom they named Jochi, and the question of his father has never been settled. The boy might have been the child of Temujin or of the Merkit man who held her, and the doubt hung over the family for the rest of the century. Temujin chose to accept him as his own, though in later years the rumour caused bitter quarrels among his sons.

Years earlier, as boys, Temujin and Jamukha had sworn an oath of brotherhood, exchanging knucklebones and later arrowheads as signs of their loyalty, and a sworn brother or anda was treated as closely as a real one. After the rescue they renewed the pledge with a feast, exchanged golden belts and horses, and for about eighteen months the two men camped together as equals. Everyone who saw the two young leaders together expected their friendship to last for the rest of their lives.

One day, as the two friends were moving camp, Jamukha spoke a riddle about where the herds should be placed, and Temujin could not decide what he meant. After talking with his mother and with Borte, he decided to leave at once, and he took his people away through the night without saying farewell. Historians believe the real cause lay in a difference of ideas, since Jamukha favoured the old order of nobles and Temujin was ready to reward talent.

As word of the departure spread, a stream of families and warriors left Jamukha's camp and followed Temujin, because they believed that he was fairer and more reliable. Among them were men who would become his best commanders, and Jamukha, who thought of them as his own people, never forgave the loss. The two men who had once shared everything now stood in opposite camps, and this was the beginning of a rivalry that would last for twenty years.

In about 1189, though the exact year is uncertain, a group of Mongol nobles and relatives gathered on the plain and chose Temujin as their khan, the title of a ruler. Each man swore to follow him in battle and to obey his orders, and in return Temujin promised to look after them and to share the spoils fairly. It was a modest beginning, since he led only a small part of the Mongols, but it was the first time that he had been recognised as a leader.

Jamukha was furious that his former friend now called himself a khan, and he gathered a large army to teach him a lesson at a place called Dalan Baljut. Temujin, who was heavily outnumbered, was defeated and driven back, although the date of the battle is uncertain and the old accounts disagree about the details. It was a bitter setback, but it was also a lesson that he would remember for a long time about the cost of weak planning.

Where other steppe rulers gave the highest posts to relatives and noblemen, Temujin chose his commanders for their talent and their loyalty, whatever their family. Former servants, herders and even captured enemies rose to lead thousands of men, among them Bo'orchu, Jelme and later the great general Muqali. The rule was simple and powerful, and it gave ambitious young men a very good reason to follow him rather than his rivals.

In 1196 the Jin rulers of northern China, who were worried about the Tatars on their border, asked Temujin and Toghrul to join them in an attack on those old enemies. The allies won a clear victory, in which the Tatar leader was killed, and the Jin court gave both men Chinese titles as a reward. For Temujin the title mattered less than the lesson that China was a rich and powerful state that could be played off against the tribes.

Temujin introduced an important rule for his men, which was that no one was to stop and gather loot until the enemy had been completely beaten. After the victory everything was gathered up and divided fairly, and even the families of men who had died in the battle received their shares. In an age when armies often fell apart as soon as they began to plunder, this discipline gave his warriors a decisive advantage.

Toghrul's son Senggum was jealous of the rising young leader, and he worked on his father's doubts until the old ruler agreed to break the alliance. In 1203 the Kereit army defeated Temujin in a hard battle in the sands, in which he lost many men, and he was wounded in the neck before he could escape. For a time it seemed that his career was over, and that the old order would triumph after all.

Temujin retreated with the survivors to the edge of a muddy lake called Baljuna, where, according to tradition, only about nineteen men remained with him. They were said to come from different tribes and even different religions, and when Temujin drank the brackish water and promised never to forget their loyalty, they drank with him and swore to share the good and the bad. The men of the Baljuna covenant were honoured for the rest of their lives.

With his strength restored, Temujin made a secret march and fell upon the Kereit camp while Toghrul's people were feasting, and the battle that followed lasted for three days. In the end the Kereit surrendered, and Toghrul, who had fled westward, was killed by a Naiman border guard who did not recognise the old ruler. Temujin welcomed the defeated Kereit into his own people, and his army was now much larger than before.

In 1204 Temujin led his army against the Naimans, the proud and well-organised people who held the lands to the west and whose ruler had joined forces with Jamukha. The battle was fierce, and Jamukha, who seems to have lost heart, withdrew in the middle of it, so that the Naiman ruler was killed and his army was overwhelmed. With this victory almost every tribe in Mongolia had now been beaten or had joined him.

Jamukha was a hunted man by now, and in about 1205 his own followers seized him and handed him over to Temujin in the hope of a reward. Temujin had the traitors executed for betraying their lord, and he offered his old friend a place at his side, but Jamukha refused, saying that there could not be two suns in the sky. He asked only for a death without bloodshed and a burial on a high place, and Temujin is said to have granted both requests.

In the spring of 1206, the chiefs of every tribe gathered beside the Onon River for a great assembly, which the Mongols called a kuriltai, and proclaimed Temujin their supreme ruler. Before them stood a banner of nine white horsetails, the standard of the new state, and he took the title Genghis Khan, the exact meaning of which scholars still debate. The scattered herders of the steppe had become, for the first time, one people with one name, the Mongols.

Nobody knows for certain what the word Genghis meant, and historians have proposed several explanations, including firm, fierce and oceanic, the last of which suggests a ruler whose power reaches in every direction. Whatever the meaning, the title gave him an authority that was higher than that of any khan who had gone before him. The new leader was now about forty-four years old, and he had spent nearly all of his life fighting for this moment.

Genghis Khan reorganised the army on a decimal system, with units of ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand men, each under its own commander. He deliberately mixed warriors from different tribes within each unit, so that a man's first loyalty would be to his comrades and to the khan, not to an old clan or an old feud. It was a quiet but revolutionary change, since it broke the power of the tribal chiefs.

After the assembly, the new khan rewarded those who had stood by him through the hard years, and the Secret History lists about ninety-five of them, each put in charge of a thousand families and warriors. Some were noblemen, but many were the humble companions of his youth, and he spoke of them with gratitude and with affection. These men became the senior leaders of a state that had not existed a year earlier.

Genghis Khan built a personal bodyguard, the keshig, which grew to about ten thousand men and which protected him at all hours of the day and night. Many of its members were the sons of commanders, so the guard also served as a school where promising young men learned to run the army and the state, and as a quiet guarantee of their fathers' good behaviour. From the ranks of the keshig came many of the officers and officials who later ran the empire.

A body of laws, later known as the Yassa, was announced and was said to apply to everyone, including the khan's own family and the nobles. It banned crimes that had caused so many feuds on the steppe, such as the kidnapping of women and the theft of animals, although historians admit that we do not know its exact contents. The idea that a law could rule even over the ruler was powerful, and it helped to turn a crowd of warriors into a state.

To keep the law in order, Genghis Khan appointed his adopted brother, Shigi Khutukhu, as chief judge, with the duty of settling disputes and recording the decisions in a register. The idea was that rulings which were written down could be checked, repeated and remembered, whereas a decision spoken once in a tent might be forgotten or distorted by the next season. The Mongols, who had never had a written law, now began to build one.

Until this time the Mongols had no writing of their own, but a Naiman official named Tata-tonga, who had been captured in the war and who kept the seal of his dead master, could write in the Uyghur script. Genghis Khan ordered him to teach the system to the princes, and the Mongol language was written down in these characters for the first time. Records, laws and letters could now be kept, copied and sent across great distances.

The Mongols followed the old religion of the Eternal Blue Sky, with its shamans and its sacred mountains, yet Genghis Khan took a genuine interest in other faiths. He freed priests, monks and teachers of all kinds from taxes and from military service, and he asked them to pray for the health of his family and the success of his state. This policy of tolerance was a practical one, because it won the loyalty of many peoples and brought clever advisers to his court.

Genghis Khan and Borte had four sons, named Jochi, Chagatai, Ogedei and Tolui, and each of them had his own character and his own ambitions. Jochi, the eldest, was shadowed by the doubt about his birth, Chagatai was strict and fond of rules, Ogedei was generous and easygoing, and Tolui was a brilliant soldier. The quarrels among them would one day decide who inherited the empire, and the problem of succession was always the weak point of the new Mongol state.

The heart of the Mongol army was the mounted archer, a rider who could shoot accurately while his horse was moving at full speed. His bow was a composite weapon, made by gluing together layers of wood, horn and animal sinew, and although it was short enough to use from the saddle, it could throw an arrow with remarkable force. Each warrior carried several such bows and many arrows, and he had practised with them since childhood.

A skilled Mongol archer could twist in the saddle and shoot to the front, to the side or even to the rear, so that retreating did not mean being defenceless. Riders are said to have released the arrow at the instant when all four of the horse's hooves were in the air, so that the jolting of the gallop did not spoil their aim. It took years of practice to reach such a standard, and most steppe boys had started long before their teens.

Mongol riders sat in firm saddles with short stirrups, which let them stand up, steady themselves and aim a bow with both hands free. Their armies could cover many kilometres a day, far more than the heavy and slow armies of Europe or China, which depended on wagons of supplies and on foot soldiers. Speed was the first of their weapons, and it often allowed them to appear in a place where nobody had expected them.

Each warrior travelled with a string of spare horses, sometimes as many as five, and he changed from one to another as the day went on so that no animal was ever worn out. This meant that an army of thirty thousand men might be followed by well over a hundred thousand horses, a huge herd that needed the best of the steppe's grass. The system made the Mongol army far faster than any rival, but it also meant that a campaign had to be planned around pasture.

The Mongol soldier travelled light, carrying strips of dried meat, hard cakes of dried milk curd and a leather water bag, so that a whole army could ride for days without lighting a single cooking fire. Foreign travellers were astonished by stories that in an emergency a rider might make a small cut in his horse's vein and drink a little of its blood, and then close the wound and ride on. Such toughness meant that the army did not need long supply trains, and that it could strike long distances from home.

Before any campaign, scouts and spies, many of them merchants who travelled freely between countries, collected information about the enemy's roads, rivers, rulers and quarrels. During a battle, commanders directed thousands of men from a hillside by waving coloured flags, beating drums and shooting whistling arrows, so that every unit knew when to advance and when to hold back. The Mongols fought as a single organised body, while many of their enemies fought as a collection of brave individuals.

One of the most famous Mongol tactics was the false retreat, in which part of the army pretended to be beaten and galloped away in apparent panic. Enemy commanders, scenting victory, ordered a chase that broke up their ranks, and the pursuers would suddenly find themselves surrounded by hidden units that swung in from both sides. The trick demanded great discipline, because a pretended flight could so easily turn into a real one if the men lost their nerve.

Each winter the Mongols organised a great hunt on a scale that no hunting party elsewhere could have matched, with thousands of riders spreading out to form a ring that might be many kilometres across. The ring then closed slowly and steadily, driving every deer and wolf inside toward the centre, and no man was allowed to break the line or let an animal escape. The hunt was in truth a rehearsal for war, and it taught the same lessons of timing, patience and obedience.

Discipline in the Mongol army was strict, and a soldier was expected to obey his officer instantly and without question, whatever the danger. Foreign travellers reported that if one man fled in battle, the other men in his group of ten could be punished, which encouraged the soldiers to watch and support each other. Rewards were also generous, and a brave soldier of humble birth might receive a share of loot, a promotion or even a high command.

When the Mongol army reached a city, it usually demanded surrender first, promising that those who submitted would be spared and would pay taxes, while those who resisted would suffer the consequences. Stories of destroyed cities travelled faster than the army itself, and fear of the Mongols won many places without a fight, though the stories may have been exaggerated in the telling. This combination of mercy and menace was a calculated policy, and its price in human suffering was often terrible.

In 1205 the Mongols began to raid Western Xia, a kingdom on the north-western edge of China, whose people, the Tangut, lived behind strong walls and defended their cities with care. The raiders were masters of the open field, where their speed and their arrows decided every battle, but they had no experience of attacking a fortified town. Learning to do so would take them several years, and it would change the whole course of their history.

In 1209 the Mongol army besieged the Xia capital and tried to drown it by redirecting the waters of the Yellow River, an ingenious plan that went badly wrong when the water also swept through the Mongol camp. Even so, the Xia ruler had seen enough of the new power on his border, and he agreed to submit, to pay tribute and to send a daughter to the khan as a bride. It was one of the first kingdoms outside the steppe to bow to the Mongols, and it was won partly by nerve and partly by luck.

In the same years the Uyghurs, a settled people whose oasis towns lay along the trade routes to the west, decided to submit to the Mongols peacefully, and their ruler was welcomed with honours. Genghis Khan treated him almost like a fifth son, and Uyghur scribes, merchants and tax collectors began to work for the Mongol state, bringing skills that the herders had never needed before. The Mongols were learning that willing partners could be worth more than conquered enemies.

Skilled engineers and craftsmen from the conquered lands, many of them Chinese and Persian, were invited or forced to join the Mongol army, and they taught it the art of the siege. Together they built catapults that could hurl heavy stones, as well as ladders, battering rams and towers, and in later campaigns they used fire weapons that relied on gunpowder. A people who had started with only horses and bows had quickly learned how to take almost any wall.

When the Jin court demanded that he kneel before its new emperor, Genghis Khan reportedly spat on the ground, mounted his horse and rode away, and from that moment war was certain. In 1211 the Mongols marched into northern China, and at a place called Yehuling they destroyed a much larger Jin army, a battle that was remembered for generations. The Jin, who had believed themselves the lords of the steppe, now realised that they faced an enemy of a very different kind.

In 1213 the Mongol columns forced their way through the narrow pass of Juyong, in the mountains north of the Jin capital, and spread out across the great plain of northern China. They ravaged the countryside, captured dozens of towns and finally surrounded the capital, where the Jin emperor agreed to pay a heavy tribute of gold, silk, horses and young people. The Mongols then withdrew, but the peace was fragile, and both sides knew that the war had hardly begun.

Soon after the peace was agreed, the Jin emperor moved his court far to the south, to the city of Kaifeng, and Genghis Khan took this as proof that the Jin did not intend to keep the bargain. The Mongols came back and besieged the old capital, Zhongdu, on the site of modern Beijing, and after months of hunger the city surrendered in 1215 and was plundered and badly burned. Chroniclers say that fires burned in the ruined palaces for weeks, a sign of how complete the destruction had been.

Among the people found in the fallen capital was Yelu Chucai, a scholar of Khitan descent who knew astronomy, several languages and the traditions of Chinese government. Genghis Khan was impressed by his learning and his courage, and the scholar remained at the Mongol court for the rest of his life, advising the khan and later his son. He argued that conquered lands could be taxed fairly and kept productive, which was far more useful than destroying them.

In 1217 Genghis Khan returned to Mongolia and left his trusted general Muqali in command of the war in China, giving him a title of prince and a free hand to act. With a small army, made up of Mongols and of soldiers from the conquered peoples, Muqali won more cities and slowly made the northern provinces secure. It showed that Genghis Khan trusted his commanders to act on their own, which let him turn his attention to the west.

Kuchlug, a Naiman prince who had escaped the Mongols years earlier, had taken over the western kingdom of Qara Khitai and had persecuted its Muslim majority, forbidding the public call to prayer. In 1218 the general Jebe defeated him, then announced in the towns that everyone was free to follow their own faith, and the people received the Mongols as liberators. With Kuchlug gone, the Mongol frontier now touched the great empire of Khwarazm, whose ruler was about to make a fatal mistake.

To the west of the new Mongol lands lay the empire of Khwarazm, which stretched from the borders of India to the Caspian Sea and was ruled by Shah Muhammad from rich cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara. Genghis Khan, who understood the value of the great caravan routes that crossed the region, proposed a treaty of friendship and open trade between the two powers. The shah agreed, but he was a suspicious man who was deeply unsure about the intentions of this new neighbour.

In 1218 a large trading caravan, sent with the khan's blessing and carrying silver, silk and furs, arrived at the border city of Otrar. The governor, Inalchuq, accused the merchants of being spies and had them executed, taking their goods, and the traditional number of dead is about four hundred and fifty, although the figure may be inflated. To a ruler who thought of trade as a sacred trust, this was an unforgivable insult.

Genghis Khan did not go to war at once but sent envoys to the shah, asking him to hand over the governor of Otrar for punishment, and giving him a chance to repair the damage peacefully. Shah Muhammad refused, and he had one of the envoys killed and the beards of the other two shaved, which was a grave insult to a man in that part of the world. By this act he had made war certain, and he was soon to learn what it meant.

Genghis Khan is said to have climbed a mountain alone and prayed to the Eternal Blue Sky for three days, asking whether the war he was about to begin was just. Then he came down and gathered an army that may have numbered somewhere between one hundred thousand and two hundred thousand men, since the sources disagree. He left his general Muqali in China and his brother Temuge in Mongolia, and he marched west with his sons.

Genghis Khan divided his army into several columns, so that the shah could not tell where the main blow would fall. Jochi led one force down the Syr Darya river, while Chagatai and Ogedei laid siege to Otrar, where the governor held out for about five months before the city was captured. The khan and his youngest son, Tolui, took the main body across the Kyzylkum desert, to appear behind the enemy where nobody had thought it was possible to travel.

In February 1220 the Mongols arrived unexpectedly outside Bukhara, a great centre of Islamic learning, and after a short siege the townspeople opened the gates, though the garrison in the citadel kept fighting until it was overwhelmed. A fire broke out in the crowded wooden city and destroyed much of it, and later Persian writers described the khan addressing the people in the great mosque, although how much of this is true is uncertain. Many of the survivors were forced to work for the army, and some of the skilled craftsmen were sent to Mongolia.

In March 1220 the army reached Samarkand, the splendid capital of the shah, whose strong walls and numerous garrison had made it seem impregnable. After only a few days the city surrendered, and the defending soldiers were killed, while thousands of craftsmen, scholars and artists were sent away to work in the Mongol lands. The Khwarazmian state, which had seemed so strong, was collapsing in a matter of months.

Shah Muhammad lost heart and fled from city to city, pursued by the Mongol generals Jebe and Subutai, who had orders to give him no rest. In the winter of 1220 or 1221 he died of illness on a small island in the Caspian Sea, where he is said to have been so poor that his burial shroud was a borrowed shirt. The empire that had been the strongest in the region was left without a leader.

At the siege of Urgench, the capital of the Khwarazm lands in the north, the brothers Jochi and Chagatai fell into such a bitter quarrel that the attack was delayed and many Mongols died. Genghis Khan angrily put their younger brother Ogedei in command, and in April 1221 the city fell, with heavy fighting from street to street. The fighting caused terrible destruction, and the quarrel between the brothers was never fully healed.

In 1221 the armies commanded by Tolui besieged Merv, Nishapur and other great cities of eastern Persia, and many of them were left in ruins with very heavy loss of life. Medieval writers gave enormous figures for the dead, in some cases more than a million, but modern historians believe that these numbers were greatly exaggerated. Nobody doubts, however, that the destruction was terrible, and that some cities never fully recovered.

Jalal ad-Din, the son of the dead shah, rallied an army and defeated a Mongol force at Parwan in 1221, one of the very few times that the Mongols were beaten in open battle. Genghis Khan himself led the pursuit, and at the bank of the Indus River the prince, with his army destroyed, leapt on his horse and plunged into the water, and swam across to safety. The khan is said to have watched with admiration and told his sons that this was how a man should behave.

Genghis Khan, who was by now over sixty, heard of a Daoist master named Changchun, who was said to be wise, holy and extremely old, and he sent a pressing invitation asking the monk to visit him. The old man, who was in his seventies, travelled for about two years across mountains, deserts and war zones to reach the camp of the khan near the Hindu Kush in 1222. His student Li Zhichang later wrote an account of the journey, which is still read today.

Genghis Khan hoped that the monk might possess an elixir of life, but the honest Changchun told him that no such medicine existed and that the best advice he could give was to live simply and rule with care. The khan was not angry but rather impressed by the answer, and he honoured the visitor, listened to his advice and freed Daoist monasteries from all taxes. It was an unusual scene, the world's greatest conqueror seeking wisdom about life from a frail old monk.

After the shah's death, the generals Jebe and Subutai did not turn back but obtained the khan's permission to ride on to the west with about twenty thousand men, to explore the lands beyond. Their expedition was part reconnaissance and part raid, and it lasted for about three years, covering distances that were almost beyond belief. They went around the southern end of the Caspian Sea, into the mountains of Azerbaijan, where they defeated the army of the kingdom of Georgia.

To cross the Caucasus mountains, the Mongol generals took advantage of the people of the walled city of Derbent, who were persuaded to show a way through the pass. On the far side they met the Alans and the Cumans, two steppe peoples who were allied, and the Mongols sent a message to the Cumans, reminding them that they were herders like the Mongols and offering them gifts. The Cumans left, the Alans were defeated, and then the Mongols turned on the Cumans too.

The defeated Cumans fled to the north-west, into the lands of the Rus, and their chief begged the Rus princes for help, warning that the Mongols would attack them next. The princes agreed to join forces and gather an army at the Dnieper River, and the Mongols sent envoys to say that they had no quarrel with the Rus and wished only to punish the Cumans. The envoys were killed, and the Rus marched out to meet an enemy they did not know.

The Mongols pretended to retreat for about nine days, drawing the Rus army after them in a long and ragged column, until it was strung out across the plain and far from its supplies. At the Kalka River in May 1223 they turned, struck with their arrows and cavalry, and routed the Rus, killing many of the princes who had led the army. It was a spectacular victory, but few people in Europe even heard the news.

After the battle at Kalka, the generals turned eastward and rode back across the great steppe, fighting a hard campaign against the Bulgars of the Volga River along the way. They had ridden thousands of kilometres, defeated several armies and learned a great deal about the geography and the politics of the lands to the west. Subutai especially stored what he had learned, and he would use it again in Europe a generation later.

In 1223 Genghis Khan began the long journey home, leaving governors in the conquered cities and taking with him the craftsmen, scholars and soldiers that he had gathered along the way. His eldest son, Jochi, who had stayed in the north after the quarrel at Urgench and had refused to answer his summons, died a few years later, although the exact date of his death is uncertain. He left behind two sons, Batu and Orda, who would rule the western part of the empire.

As he grew older, Genghis Khan knew that the empire needed a clear plan for the future, and he asked his sons to say who should follow him. Since Jochi and Chagatai could not agree with each other, he chose his third son, Ogedei, who was kind, generous and well liked by the nobles. The decision was wise in the short term, but it did not solve the deeper problem of how the empire would be divided among the family.

Western Xia had refused to send soldiers to help in the war against Khwarazm, and the old accounts say that its leaders answered the khan's call with contempt. In 1226, although he was well over sixty, Genghis Khan led an army against the Tangut kingdom and swept through its towns and its desert strongholds one by one. The campaign was meant to settle an old debt and to remove an enemy who stood on the road to China.

During the campaign, while hunting wild horses on the plain, Genghis Khan was thrown from his horse and badly shaken, and that night a high fever came on. His advisers begged him to return home and rest, but the khan insisted that the army should not retreat, since the Tangut would say that the Mongols had been afraid. It was a proud decision from a man who had spent his whole life refusing to turn back.

Genghis Khan died in August 1227, at the age of about sixty-five, while his army was still besieging the last Tangut cities, and his death was kept quiet until the campaign was won. Historians have suggested many causes, including the effects of his fall, a fever, an infection or a wound, but the sources are unclear and we shall probably never know for sure. According to tradition his last advice to his sons was to defeat the Jin by marching through Song territory.

His body was carried back across the steppe to his homeland, and his burial was kept so secret that it has remained a mystery to the present day. Legends say that the funeral party killed everyone they met on the road, and that horses were driven over the grave to hide it, although these tales may well have been invented to explain why nobody found the tomb. Many expeditions have searched for it in modern times, including some with satellite photographs, and none has succeeded.

For two years the empire was run by Tolui, the youngest son, who acted as regent and who inherited the family's homeland, according to the Mongol custom that gave the youngest son the hearth of his father. Tolui was a fine general, popular with the army, and he could have tried to seize the throne for himself, but he chose to wait for the assembly. It was an act of loyalty that kept the young empire from splitting at its most dangerous moment.

In 1229 the princes and generals gathered at the great assembly and chose Ogedei, as Genghis Khan had wished, to be the second great khan of the Mongols. He was about forty-three years old, a large, cheerful man who loved feasting and was known for his generosity, and the ceremony was held with the old rituals, including the gift of horses and the oath of loyalty. A smooth change of ruler at this time showed that the empire could survive the death of its founder.

Ogedei decided to finish the war against the Jin, and he made an alliance with the Song dynasty of southern China, which wished to take revenge on the northern state for old humiliations. After a long siege of the city of Caizhou in 1234, the Jin were destroyed, and their last emperor took his own life rather than surrender. The Mongols now held the whole of northern China, and they quickly turned against their former allies, the Song.

Around 1235 Ogedei ordered the building of a permanent capital at Karakorum, in the valley of the Orkhon River in the heart of Mongolia, with walls, a palace and stores for grain. Craftsmen from many countries, including China and Persia, came to build and decorate it, and caravans brought food from distant provinces to feed the people who lived there. It was a remarkable place, a stone-and-wood town in the middle of a sea of grass.

Some Mongol nobles argued that the farmland of northern China was of no use to the Mongols and should be turned into pasture for their herds, and a good deal of damage was done on this principle. Yelu Chucai persuaded Ogedei that it would be far more profitable to leave the farmers in place and tax them, and a census of the northern population was carried out to make it possible. His argument is often said to have saved many lives and to have made Mongol rule in China more lasting.

At another great assembly in 1235, the Mongol leaders decided on a series of new campaigns on several fronts, which showed how ambitious the empire had become. They planned to fight the Song in southern China, to press on into Korea, and to send an enormous army toward the west, under the command of the grandson Batu and the veteran general Subutai. The next five years would carry Mongol riders further than anyone in Europe could have imagined.

In 1236 a huge army set out from the Mongol lands toward the west, led in name by Batu, a grandson of Genghis Khan, and in practice by the veteran general Subutai. Many of the other princes of the family came along, and the army, with its allies from conquered peoples, probably numbered tens of thousands of men. The planning was shrewd and careful, because Subutai had already ridden through these lands years before.

The Mongols began by crushing the Volga Bulgars, a wealthy trading people whose cities lay on the great river, and their capital was captured and badly damaged. They also hunted down the Cumans, a steppe people who were old enemies, and many of the survivors scattered, some of them to the west and some of them to the south. By the end of 1237 there was no strong power left between the Mongols and the Russian principalities.

The land of the Rus, which was divided among many rival princes who were more concerned with their own quarrels than with the common defence, seemed an easy target. The Mongols did something that nobody expected and attacked in midwinter, when the frozen rivers became broad highways through the forests and the horses could cross marshes that were impassable in summer. Their knowledge of the seasons turned the hardest time of the year into an advantage.

When the Mongols reached the city of Ryazan, they demanded a tenth of everything its people owned, and the prince, who had hoped for help from his neighbours that never arrived, refused. After a siege of about five days in December 1237, the city was stormed and burned, and the chroniclers wrote with horror about the ruins. The news of its fate travelled fast, and it frightened the other cities of the north.

Early in 1238 the Mongols defeated the army of Vladimir and took the fortress of Kolomna, and then they captured a small wooden town named Moscow, which was still unimportant at that time. They had no way of knowing that this modest place would grow into the capital of a great state, which would one day challenge their own heirs. The army then turned toward the principal city of the region, the splendid and wealthy Vladimir.

Grand Prince Yuri had left his capital, Vladimir, in the hands of his family and gone north to raise an army, trusting that the strong walls would protect the city for a while. In February 1238 the Mongols brought up their siege engines, battered through the defences and stormed in, and many of the people who had taken refuge in the great cathedral perished in the fire. Vladimir was one of the most splendid cities of the Rus, and it never regained its old importance.

A few weeks later, on 4 March 1238, the Mongol scouts found Grand Prince Yuri's camp beside the Sit River, and the army struck before the Rus could form their ranks. The battle was brief and one-sided, the Rus were surrounded and cut down, and Yuri himself was killed. With this defeat the military strength of the north-eastern Rus was broken, and no prince could stand against the invaders.

A small town named Kozelsk, ruled by a boy prince, held out against the Mongols for about seven weeks in the spring of 1238, and it cost them dearly in time and in lives. Soon afterwards the army turned back toward the steppe, probably because the thaw was turning the ground to mud and the horses needed rest and grass, so the great northern city of Novgorod was spared. The Mongols are said to have called Kozelsk the Evil City, which was a kind of backhanded tribute to its courage.

After resting for more than a year in the grasslands to the south, the Mongols returned in 1239 and took one city after another, and in late 1240 they reached the ancient capital of Kyiv. Its citizens defended the walls bravely, and the commander Dmitr was said to be wounded but spared by Batu in admiration of his courage, but the city fell in December 1240 after a hard siege. Years later a papal envoy found only about two hundred houses standing and many skulls lying in the fields.

After the conquest the princes of the Rus kept their lands but had to travel to the Mongol court to receive their titles and pay regular tribute to the khan of the Golden Horde. The arrangement lasted for more than two hundred years, and while some historians describe it as a crushing yoke that held Russia back, others see a more complex relationship that even helped Moscow to grow. The truth probably lies somewhere between those two views, and the debate among scholars continues.

Thousands of Cumans, driven from their pastures by the Mongol advance, fled westward and were given shelter in Hungary by King Bela IV, who hoped to gain useful soldiers and converts. The Mongols saw this as a hostile act, since they considered the Cumans their own runaway subjects, and they sent messengers demanding that the refugees be handed back. The Hungarians treated the envoys badly, and the Mongols took their answer as a declaration of war.

In the early months of 1241 the Mongols divided their army into several groups that moved on separate paths, so that their enemies could never be certain where the main blow would fall. One force rode north into Poland, burning towns as it went, while the main army, led by Batu and Subutai, crossed the Carpathian mountains into Hungary through the passes, which had been left poorly defended. The plan was audacious, and it relied on perfect timing across hundreds of kilometres.

In Poland the Mongol columns raided far and wide, sacking the towns of Sandomierz and Krakow, whose people fled before them, and the Polish princes, who were divided and unprepared, mostly withdrew to the mountains or went abroad. Duke Henry of Silesia hastened to gather an army before the invaders could spread any further into central Europe. He hoped to join forces with the king of Bohemia, who was marching to his aid.

On 9 April 1241, near the town of Legnica, the army of Duke Henry II, made up of Poles, Germans and knights of the military orders, met the Mongols on an open plain before the king of Bohemia could arrive. The Mongols pretended to retreat, the heavy knights chased them out of formation, and then the Mongols turned around and cut them down, killing the duke himself. Although the Mongols did not conquer Poland, the battle showed that the knights of Europe were no match for the horse archers of Asia.

Two days later, on 11 April 1241, the Hungarian army, camped behind a ring of wagons near the Sajo River, woke to find the Mongols crossing the river at dawn and bombarding them with stone-throwers and fire. The Hungarians were surrounded, but the Mongols left a gap on purpose, and many soldiers poured through it and were cut down in the marshes as they ran. It was one of the most complete victories in the whole of Mongol history.

King Bela escaped from the battlefield and fled across the country until he reached the Adriatic coast, where he took refuge on an island, while the Mongols burned the town of Pest and spread out across the plains. They spent the summer and the winter raiding, and in the bitter cold of the new year they crossed the frozen Danube, hunting the king. Historians estimate that between a fifth and a half of the Hungarian people were killed or driven away.

In December 1241 the great khan Ogedei died in Karakorum, reportedly after a night of heavy drinking, and the news travelled thousands of kilometres across the steppe to the army in Europe. Every prince of the family had a claim to be involved in the choice of the next khan, and none of them wanted to be absent when it was made. The war in the west suddenly seemed less important than the struggle for the throne.

In 1242 the Mongol armies turned around and left Europe, to the astonishment of those who had expected to be conquered, and historians have argued about the reason ever since. The death of Ogedei was probably the most important cause, although some scholars point also to the limited grassland of Hungary, which could not feed so many horses, and to the castles that were still holding out. Europe was lucky, but it was certainly not saved by the strength of its own armies.

Batu did not go back to Karakorum but made his own capital, Sarai, on the lower Volga River, where he ruled over a large territory that stretched from the Carpathians to Siberia. This realm, later known as the Golden Horde, was in practice almost independent, and its khans ruled the Russian principalities for a very long time. It was the first of the empire's pieces to drift away from the centre.

The raid caused deep alarm in Europe, where writers called the Mongols Tatars and claimed that they were demons from Tartarus, the underworld of the ancient myths. In 1245 Pope Innocent IV, who was anxious to learn who these people were and whether they could be turned into allies, sent a monk named John of Plano Carpini on the long journey to the Mongol court. His report would be the first detailed account of the Mongols by a European.

After Ogedei's death, his widow Toregene took charge of the empire as regent, a position that was recognised under Mongol custom, and she held it for about five years. She dismissed many of her husband's advisers, including the veteran scholar Yelu Chucai, and filled the government with people loyal to herself, while she worked to secure the throne for her eldest son, Guyuk. She was both a capable administrator and a skilful politician, and she held her enemies in check.

Mongol women enjoyed a freedom and an authority that astonished many foreign visitors, who came from societies where women were kept much more strictly at home. They managed the herds, the carts and the camps while the men were away at war, and the great ladies commanded their own households and advisers and owned property in their own right. Toregene and her successors were the most visible examples of a tradition that ran through ordinary life on the steppe.

In 1246 an enormous assembly was held near Karakorum, with thousands of guests who came from distant countries, and Guyuk was formally chosen as the third great khan. Among the visitors was the monk John of Plano Carpini, who had travelled for months from Europe to deliver the pope's letter, and who described the ceremony and the great tents with wonder. Guyuk replied to the pope in haughty language, telling him that if he wanted peace, he must come in person and submit.

Guyuk was in poor health even when he was chosen, and he died in 1248, after ruling for only two years, while travelling toward the west. He may have been preparing to confront his cousin Batu, who had never accepted his leadership, and the sources suggest that relations between the two were extremely tense. The empire now faced a dangerous quarrel between the family of Ogedei and the family of Tolui.

Sorghaghtani Beki, the widow of Genghis Khan's youngest son, Tolui, came from the Kereit people and followed the Christian faith, but she supported Muslims, Buddhists and Daoists with equal fairness. She raised four extraordinary sons, Mongke, Khubilai, Hulegu and Ariq Boke, and she made sure that they were educated, trained to govern and acquainted with the customs of other peoples. Persian historians later wrote of her in terms of great admiration, and it is said that she was an excellent politician.

With the support of Batu in the west and of his own mother's careful planning, Mongke was elected great khan in 1251, and the leadership of the empire passed from the line of Ogedei to the line of Tolui. He moved quickly to remove his rivals, and a number of princes and officials who had opposed him were arrested, tried and executed. The empire's brief age of open competition for power had ended, and Mongke was not a man to tolerate resistance.

Mongke was a serious, frugal and hard-working ruler who had little patience for waste or for officials who enriched themselves at the expense of the peasants. He ordered a census of the empire, so that taxes could be fixed fairly according to what people owned, and he tried to stop the abuses of the tax collectors and of the merchants who lent money at harsh rates. His reforms made the empire more regular, and they also provided money for the wars that he planned.

In 1254 a Flemish friar named William of Rubruck, who had been sent east by King Louis of France, reached Karakorum after a journey of many months across the steppe. He wrote a lively account in which he observed that the city was not much larger than a village near Paris, but that its streets were filled with merchants and craftsmen from China, Persia, Russia and Europe. His honest and curious report is one of the best sources that we have about the capital.

In front of the khan's palace stood a magnificent silver tree, made by a French goldsmith named Guillaume Boucher, who had been captured in the war in Hungary and brought to Karakorum. Pipes ran through the trunk and branches, and when it was time to serve drinks, servants blew a horn and the tree poured wine, rice liquor and fermented mare's milk into silver bowls. The tree was a fine example of how the empire gathered craftsmen from every country and set them to work on the same project.

In May 1254, Mongke arranged a formal debate at his court, in which Christians, Muslims and Buddhists were invited to defend their beliefs in front of him, according to rules that he laid down. The friar Rubruck reports that afterwards the khan likened the faiths to the fingers of a hand, which God had made different from one another, and that no one was to threaten anybody else. The scene is one of the most remarkable episodes in the religious history of the thirteenth century.

Mongke planned two great campaigns for the 1250s, which were intended to complete the work that Genghis Khan had begun. One army, led partly by his brother Khubilai, would continue the war against the Song dynasty in southern China, while another, under his younger brother Hulegu, would march into western Asia and bring the Muslim lands under Mongol rule. Both armies were enormous, and they included engineers, doctors and astronomers as well as soldiers.

In the mountains of northern Persia, the Nizari Ismailis, a religious community whom their enemies called the Assassins, had held a chain of fortresses for generations, including the famous castle of Alamut. Hulegu's army, supported by catapults and Chinese engineers, forced their leader to surrender in 1256, and the fortresses were destroyed. The scholar Juvayni, who served the Mongols, was allowed to look through the library at Alamut and to save some of its books.

Hulegu sent a message to the caliph, al-Musta'sim, who was the religious leader of the Sunni Muslim world and ruled from Baghdad, ordering him to submit and to pull down his city's defences. The caliph, whose family, the Abbasids, had ruled for more than five hundred years, refused to believe that anyone would dare to attack him, and his advisers quarrelled over what to do. He had neglected his army, and he was now relying on the fame of his name.

In January 1258 several Mongol columns closed in on Baghdad from different directions, and the engineers built a ditch and a palisade around the city so that nobody could escape. Catapults and other siege machines, some of them worked by Chinese specialists, bombarded the walls for about two weeks, and the defenders, who were hopelessly outnumbered, could do little in reply. On 10 February the caliph came out of the city with his sons and officials and surrendered.

The Mongols entered Baghdad and sacked it for about a week, and the caliph was executed soon afterwards, though the accounts differ about exactly how he died. Many thousands of people were killed, with estimates ranging from perhaps a hundred thousand to several times that number, and historians are unable to agree on the true figure. The fall of the Abbasid capital was felt as a blow across the entire Muslim world.

Hulegu's chief wife, Doquz Khatun, was a Christian, and she asked that the Christian community of Baghdad should be spared, so a number of churches and their congregations were protected. The libraries of the city were badly damaged, and a famous story says that the Tigris ran black with the ink of the books that were thrown into it, although historians question how far this is true. What is certain is that many centuries of accumulated learning were lost or scattered in a few days.

In early 1260 the Mongol army marched into Syria, supported by Christian allies from Armenia and Georgia and led by the general Kitbuqa, who was himself a Christian of the Nestorian faith. Aleppo was captured after a short and fierce siege, and Damascus, the great Syrian capital, surrendered without a fight, so that almost the whole of the Middle East seemed to lie open to the Mongols. Only Egypt, ruled by the Mamluk sultans, remained to be conquered, and its rulers prepared for the worst.

In August 1259 Mongke died while directing the campaign against the Song in China, perhaps of dysentery or cholera, and the news soon reached Hulegu in the Middle East. Since a new great khan had to be chosen, and since his own brothers were involved in the quarrel, Hulegu took most of his army back toward Persia, partly because the pastures in Syria could not support so many horses. He left Kitbuqa behind with only a small force to hold the lands that had just been won.

On 3 September 1260, at a place called Ain Jalut in Palestine, the Mamluk army of Egypt, commanded by the sultan Qutuz and the general Baibars, met Kitbuqa's much smaller force and defeated it, killing the Mongol general. The Mamluks had chosen the ground with care and used the Mongols' own favourite tactic, a pretended retreat, to draw their opponents into a trap. It was the first time that a Mongol army had been beaten in a major battle in the west.
