The Mongols never succeeded in conquering Egypt, and the Mamluks held the border in a series of later battles, so that the westward expansion that had begun with Genghis Khan came to an end. Hulegu wanted revenge for the defeat, but he was soon drawn into a war with his cousin Berke, the ruler of the Golden Horde, who had become a Muslim and was angry about the sack of Baghdad. The quarrels within the family were now becoming more serious than the wars against foreign enemies.

Khubilai was born in 1215, the grandson of Genghis Khan, and under the influence of his remarkable mother he grew up with a lively curiosity about the world beyond the steppe. When his brother Mongke gave him the governorship of northern China, he gathered around him Chinese scholars, Buddhist monks and a young Tibetan teacher named Pagpa, and he listened carefully to what they told him. He understood that a country as large and as old as China could not be ruled simply by terror.

When Mongke died, the empire had no obvious heir, and in 1260 two of his brothers were proclaimed great khan within a few weeks of each other, in different places. Khubilai was acclaimed at his own assembly at Kaiping in northern China, while his younger brother Ariq Boke was elected at the old capital, Karakorum, by the nobles who preferred the traditional way of life. The quarrel between the two brothers was to shatter the unity of the empire for good.

The two brothers fought a bitter civil war that lasted from 1260 until 1264, and the outcome was decided largely by supplies, since Karakorum depended on grain from China that Khubilai now controlled. Hunger and defeat in the field finally forced Ariq Boke to surrender, and he was later pardoned, although he died soon afterward. The war was a turning point, because the other khanates of the empire were not willing to accept Khubilai as their ruler.

In 1267 Khubilai began to build a vast new capital, called Khanbaliq or Dadu, on the site of the modern city of Beijing, and he employed Chinese and Muslim designers to plan it. The city was laid out as a regular grid, with wide straight avenues, great walls, gates, canals, temples and a palace complex of extraordinary size. It would eventually become one of the largest and most splendid cities on the face of the earth.

In 1271 Khubilai gave his government in China the dynastic name Yuan, taken from an ancient Chinese book of wisdom, and he began to follow the ceremonies and the rituals of a Chinese emperor, including temples for his ancestors. He wanted to be both a Mongol khan and a legitimate ruler of China, a difficult balance that he handled with considerable skill, though many of his Chinese subjects never fully accepted him. The new dynasty included a vast territory that stretched from Manchuria in the east to Tibet in the west.

The Yuan government gave people different rights according to their origins, with the Mongols at the top, their foreign helpers next, then the northern Chinese, and the people of the former Song lands at the bottom. Many Chinese scholars lost their old positions when the traditional examinations were suspended, although some served Khubilai with distinction. Historians still debate how rigidly this system was applied, but it left deep resentment.

The Song city of Xiangyang, which held out against a Mongol siege from 1268 to 1273, was one of the strongest fortresses in China, and it blocked the road to the south. In the end, engineers from Persia built powerful counterweight catapults that could throw much heavier stones than any earlier machine, and the walls and the courage of the defenders finally gave way. The fall of the city opened the way into the rich heartland of the Song.

In 1276 the great Song capital of Lin'an, the modern Hangzhou, surrendered to the Mongol general Bayan, and the child emperor and his grandmother, the empress dowager, handed over the imperial seal. Because the city yielded peacefully it was spared the sack that had fallen on so many others, and it remained a rich and elegant place that astonished later visitors. Marco Polo would later describe its canals, bridges and crowded markets with wonder, calling it the finest city in the world.

A few loyal Song officials continued to resist from a floating court of ships off the southern coast, with a child emperor at their head, until the decisive naval battle of Yamen in 1279. The Song fleet was defeated, the minister Lu Xiufu is said to have jumped into the sea with the young emperor in his arms, and the dynasty came to an end. It was the first time that all of China had been ruled by a foreign people.

To feed his huge new capital, Khubilai repaired and extended the roads and the great waterways, including the Grand Canal, so that grain from the fertile south could reach the north in large barges. The astronomer and engineer Guo Shoujing planned some of the new sections, and the finished canal served China for many centuries, long after the Mongols had gone. It was a practical reminder that conquest was only the first step in building an empire.

By the late thirteenth century a traveller could cross the whole of Asia, from the shores of the Pacific to the Black Sea, without leaving lands that were ruled by Mongols, something that had never been possible before. Later historians called this period the Mongol Peace, although the empire was often at war with itself, and the peace was often unevenly kept. Even so, the effect on trade, travel and the exchange of ideas was very large.

The Mongols built a network of relay stations, called the yam, along the main roads of the empire, each one kept stocked with fresh horses, food and places to sleep at intervals of a day's ride. A royal messenger could change horses at every station and keep riding for days, and in an emergency he could cover perhaps as much as three hundred kilometres in a single day. News and orders could thus cross the empire far more quickly than they could anywhere else in the world.

Officials, envoys and some favoured merchants carried a metal tablet called a paiza, usually engraved with a command in the name of the great khan, which worked rather like a modern passport. Its holder had the right to food, fresh horses and shelter at every station, and anyone who refused or mistreated him risked severe punishment. The tablets were made of gold, silver or bronze, according to the rank of the bearer.

The Mongol rulers wanted the roads to be safe for merchants, because trade brought them taxes and luxuries, so they punished robbers severely and watched the main routes. Local officials were held responsible for any theft that occurred in their district, which gave them a strong reason to keep order, and travellers who passed through reported with surprise how secure the journey had become. Merchants also received loans from Mongol princes to finance their caravans, in partnerships that were profitable to both sides.

Caravans carried silk, tea, spices, silver, porcelain and horses across the continent, and the great markets of cities such as Tabriz, Samarkand and Khanbaliq were crowded with goods from places that most of the buyers had never heard of. Inns for travellers and their animals appeared at regular distances along the roads, and merchants from Venice, Genoa, Persia and China did business with one another. Few earlier empires had been so interested in trade or had done so much to protect its routes.

The Yuan government issued paper banknotes stamped with a red seal and required everyone to accept them instead of silver and copper coins, which were heavy and awkward to carry over long distances. Visitors from Europe, where such a thing was unknown, were astonished that people would accept paper for goods, and for a time the system worked very well. But when later rulers printed too many notes to pay their bills, the money steadily lost its value and the people lost confidence in it.

Around 1271 a seventeen-year-old Venetian named Marco Polo set out with his father and uncle, both merchants who had already visited the great khan, on an overland journey through Persia and the mountains of Central Asia. After about three and a half years on the road, they reached the summer capital of Khubilai Khan, who received them kindly. The young man learned languages quickly, and the khan began to give him missions.

Marco Polo spent about seventeen years in Asia, and he was sent on missions to distant provinces and to other courts, so that he saw more of the empire than most of its subjects. In about 1291 the Polo family sailed from China escorting a Mongol princess who was to marry the ruler of Persia, a voyage that lasted more than two years, and in 1295 they reached Venice after twenty-four years away. His family hardly recognised him, according to the old story, and had to be convinced of who he was.

A few years later, Marco Polo was captured during a war between Venice and Genoa, and in a Genoese prison he told his story to a fellow prisoner, the writer Rustichello, who wrote it down. The book became enormously popular, and it inspired later explorers, but some scholars point out that he does not mention tea or the Great Wall and wonder how much he saw himself. Others reply that he mentioned many accurate details that no stay-at-home could have known.

Rabban Sauma was a Christian monk born in the area of modern Beijing, who had travelled westward as a pilgrim and had been sent in 1287 by the Mongol ruler of Persia on a diplomatic mission to Europe. He met King Philip of France and King Edward of England, and wrote an account in the Persian language of what he saw, in which he marvelled at Paris and its university. Perhaps the first person from the Far East to see western Europe, he showed that the road ran both ways.

The Mongol rulers valued skill wherever they found it, and they gathered scholars, doctors, astronomers and craftsmen from China, Persia, Tibet, India and Europe to work in their courts. Many of these people came as captives or as servants, but they were often treated well and rewarded generously, because the rulers cared much more about talent than about a man's birthplace. The result was an unusual mixing of knowledge that would have been unlikely in a more closed society.

In 1259 Hulegu founded a large observatory at Maragha, in north-western Persia, and put the great scholar Nasir al-Din Tusi in charge, with a library and astronomers from several countries. They made careful observations and produced astronomical tables that were used for centuries, and some historians believe that their mathematical ideas later reached Europe. It was a remarkable example of rulers who were famous for war paying for the study of pure science.

In Khanbaliq, Khubilai employed both Persian astronomers, who brought instruments from the west, and Chinese ones, among them the brilliant Guo Shoujing, who designed new tools and built observatories. In 1281 their work produced the Shoushi calendar, which measured the year at 365 days, 5 hours and 49 minutes, exactly the figure used by the calendar that Europe would adopt three centuries later. Scholars from two great traditions of science had learned from each other, and the result was one of the best calendars in the world.

Physicians from Persia, China and other countries exchanged knowledge in the Mongol courts, and hospitals in several cities employed doctors who had been trained in different traditions. The Persian physician and minister Rashid al-Din arranged for Chinese medical works, including ones on the pulse, to be translated into Persian, so that their ideas could be read in the Middle East. Not everything that was shared in this way was correct, but the sharing itself was enormously valuable.

Around 1300 the Persian minister Rashid al-Din was commissioned by the Mongol ruler of Persia to write a history of the Mongols, and the project grew into something much greater, a history of the whole known world. He consulted experts from China, India and Europe and used the best sources that he could find, so the Compendium of Chronicles is often described as the first world history. It remains one of our most valuable sources for the history of the Mongols and their neighbours.

Chinese potters in the town of Jingdezhen began to decorate their white porcelain with a deep blue colour, which came from cobalt that merchants brought from Persia. The new blue-and-white porcelain, whose designs were often adapted to suit the tastes of customers in the Middle East, was loved from the moment it appeared, and it soon spread across Asia. Without the Mongol trade routes, the combination of the two traditions might never have been made.

In 1294 the Mongol ruler of Persia, whose treasury was empty, tried to introduce paper money on the Chinese model, and he even had the notes printed with a few Chinese characters. The merchants refused to accept them, the markets closed, and the riots that followed forced him to withdraw the whole scheme within a matter of weeks. It showed that a good idea from one culture does not always work in another.

In northern China the Mongols came across gunpowder weapons such as rockets, fire arrows and bombs thrown by catapults, and they used them in a number of their later sieges. Historians think that knowledge of gunpowder, and probably some of the devices that used it, spread westward along the routes that the Mongol armies and engineers followed, although the details of the transfer are unclear. The weapon would eventually change the whole nature of war in Europe, in Asia and in the Middle East.

Khubilai dreamed of a single writing system that could record all the languages of his empire, from Mongolian to Chinese and Persian, so in 1269 he asked the Tibetan monk Pagpa to design one. The new Phags-pa script was used on official documents, coins and the tablets that were carried by messengers, but it never became widely popular, and it was dropped after the Mongols left China. It was a very ambitious idea, though perhaps not a surprising one for a ruler of so many different peoples.

In 1330 a court official named Hu Sihui presented a book on food and health to the Yuan emperor, in which he described the diets and recipes that were fashionable at the palace. It included dishes with lamb, spices and ingredients that had come from Mongolia, Persia, Central Asia and China, and it shows how the empire's trade had changed the tables of the rich. The kitchen of the palace was another place where the different peoples of the empire met and mixed.

In 1274 Khubilai sent a fleet of several hundred ships, built and manned largely by his Korean subjects, to attack the islands of Japan, and the troops landed near Hakata Bay. They fought the samurai for a day, using explosive missiles that the defenders had never seen, but at night a storm blew up, and the commanders withdrew to the ships and sailed away. Many of the vessels were lost on the voyage home, and thousands of men failed to return.

The Japanese leaders were certain that the Mongols would return, so they spent the next few years building a long stone wall around Hakata Bay and gathering their warriors along the coast. When Khubilai sent envoys to demand that Japan submit, the rulers of the Kamakura government had them executed, which made another invasion certain. Both sides were now determined, and the stage was set for a much larger fight.

In 1281 two enormous fleets, which carried well over a hundred thousand men according to most accounts, set out for Japan from Korea and southern China, but the attack was badly co-ordinated and the stone wall held the landing back. In August a great typhoon struck, wrecking much of the fleet, and the Japanese later spoke of it as the kamikaze, or the divine wind. Many of the ships had been hastily built for river use, and they were not strong enough for the open sea.

The Tran dynasty of Vietnam fought off the Mongols three times, in 1258, 1285 and again in 1287 to 1288, using guerrilla tactics, the heat and disease of the jungle and the knowledge of their own country. In the last war the general Tran Hung Dao planted iron-tipped stakes in the bed of the Bach Dang River at high tide, so that when the water fell, the Mongol ships were trapped and destroyed. The Vietnamese nevertheless sent tribute, which let both sides claim a kind of victory.

In 1293 Khubilai sent a fleet to the island of Java to punish a king who had insulted his envoy, but by the time the force arrived the king was already dead. The Mongols were drawn into a local quarrel, and a clever prince named Raden Wijaya, having used them to defeat his rival, turned on them and drove them out of the country. He went on to found the Majapahit empire, which became the strongest power in the islands for a long time.

In the hot and humid forests of Southeast Asia, the Mongol cavalry lost much of its strength, because the horses fell sick, the pastures were poor and the enemy knew the terrain far better. Mongol armies did take the Burmese kingdom of Pagan in the 1280s, but they could not hold the jungle lands, and each campaign was costly. Wherever the grass ended, the old advantages of the Mongols began to melt away.

In his last years Khubilai suffered many sorrows, among them the deaths of his beloved wife Chabi and of the son whom he had chosen as heir, and he grew heavy, ill and increasingly lonely. He died in February 1294, aged about seventy-eight, after more than thirty years as great khan, and was buried in secret in the Mongol homeland. He was the last ruler whom all the khanates even nominally recognised as their overlord.

By the time Khubilai died, the empire had effectively split into four great khanates, each ruled by a different branch of the family, and each was pursuing its own interests. They were the Yuan in China and Mongolia, the Golden Horde in the Russian steppe, the Ilkhanate in Persia and the Chagatai khanate in Central Asia. The prince Kaidu, from the family of Ogedei, had fought Khubilai for more than thirty years, and his long rebellion ended only after his death in 1301.

In the western khanates, the Mongol rulers gradually adopted the religion of the people they ruled, which in most cases was Islam. Berke of the Golden Horde had become a Muslim in the 1250s, Ghazan of the Ilkhanate converted in 1295, and Ozbeg Khan made Islam the official religion of the Golden Horde in 1313. These conversions helped the Mongols to rule, but they also tied them more closely to the lands where they lived and made them less Mongol.

As the generations passed, the Mongol rulers in each land slowly took on the language, dress and customs of the people whom they ruled, in a process that historians call assimilation. The Yuan emperors became more Chinese, the Ilkhans became more Persian and the khans of the Golden Horde spoke the Turkic language of their subjects, and the Mongol language faded from the courts. The conquerors, in other words, were being gently conquered in return by the peoples they ruled.

After Khubilai the Yuan court was often shaken by quarrels over the throne, and many emperors reigned for only a few years, so that the government drifted without a firm hand. Paper money continued to lose its value, taxes were heavy, and in the 1340s the Yellow River burst its banks and caused terrible floods and famines. In the countryside, hungry people started to ask whether the dynasty had lost the favour of Heaven.

In 1351 groups of rebels who wore red headscarves, and who are known as the Red Turbans, rose against the Yuan dynasty, and the revolt soon spread across much of China. One of the most successful leaders, Zhu Yuanzhang, was an orphan from a poor family who had once been a beggar and a Buddhist monk, and who proved to be an able commander. He gradually defeated the other rebel leaders as well as the Yuan armies sent against him.

In 1368 Zhu Yuanzhang proclaimed himself emperor of the new Ming dynasty, and his army marched on the capital, Khanbaliq, where the last Yuan emperor, Toghon Temur, decided to flee north with his court rather than fight. Mongol rule in China had lasted for almost a hundred years since the founding of the Yuan, and the Mongols returned to the steppe. A government of Mongols, later called the Northern Yuan, continued to rule in Mongolia for some time.

A terrible new disease, which was later named the Black Death, seems to have begun in Central Asia, and a study published in 2022 found plague in the graves of a cemetery near Lake Issyk-Kul that dated from 1338 and 1339. The evidence suggests that the plague spread from those mountain valleys along the same trade routes that carried silk, spices and ideas. The roads that had brought the world together now carried the deadliest illness in its history.

In 1346 an army of the Golden Horde besieged Caffa, a port on the Crimean coast that belonged to merchants from Genoa, and plague broke out among the besiegers. An Italian writer reported that the Mongols threw the bodies of the dead over the walls with catapults, although historians doubt that this was the way the plague reached the town. Soon afterwards, ships left the port for the Mediterranean, carrying people, goods and rats that were infected.

In 1347 the plague reached Sicily and the ports of Italy, and then it spread across the whole of Europe in a few years, killing at least a quarter of the people and perhaps a half in some places. The exact figures are uncertain, but the shock was immense, and whole villages were left empty while the survivors struggled to bury the dead. The disease also struck the Middle East, and probably China, which suffered its own heavy losses.

The Mongol states in the west were already falling apart before the plague, and the disease only made their problems worse. The Ilkhanate in Persia had collapsed in 1335, when its ruler died without an heir and the nobles started to fight each other, and the Chagatai khanate in Central Asia later split into two parts. Armies dwindled, trade routes closed and the great network that the Mongols had built began to unravel.

A new conqueror, Timur, who was of Turkic origin and came from the area of Samarkand, rose to power in Central Asia in the 1370s, and he took Genghis Khan as his model. Because he was not a descendant of the great khan, he ruled in the name of a puppet prince of the Mongol family, and he defeated the Golden Horde in the 1390s and burned its capital. He also fought in India and Persia and left a trail of ruined cities that recalled the age of Genghis.

Under repeated blows the Golden Horde broke up into smaller khanates, including those of Kazan, Astrakhan and Crimea, while Moscow, once a tiny wooden fort, grew steadily stronger. In 1480 Ivan III refused to pay tribute to the khan, and the two armies faced each other across the Ugra River for weeks until the khan, Akhmat, gave up and led his men home. The old Mongol rule over Russia was over, though the Crimean khanate lasted until 1783.

In 1526 a prince from Central Asia named Babur, who claimed descent from both Timur and Genghis Khan, defeated the sultan of Delhi at the battle of Panipat and founded a new empire in India. The word Mughal is simply the Persian way of saying Mongol, and the dynasty took great pride in this ancestry, though by then it spoke Persian and followed Islam. Its rulers built magnificent works, including the Taj Mahal, and they governed much of India for more than three centuries.

There is no doubt that the Mongol conquests killed a very large number of people, since cities were destroyed, farms were abandoned and whole populations were uprooted. Medieval writers gave figures that run into the millions for single cities, but modern historians regard many of these as exaggerated, and their own estimates for the whole period differ enormously. Even the most careful scholars admit that the true totals can never be known with any certainty.

In some regions, especially in parts of Persia and Central Asia, the irrigation channels on which all farming depended were wrecked, and the farmers who knew how to repair them were killed or had fled. Without water the fields turned to dust, and in several places the land took generations to recover, while some famous cities such as Merv never regained their old importance. The damage done in a few years of war could last for many centuries afterward.

At the same time, the Mongol empire brought distant peoples into contact on a scale that had never been seen before, so that the goods, the ideas and the stories of Asia reached Europe in a stream. Marco Polo's book was read by merchants, mapmakers and dreamers, and Columbus himself owned a copy, which he covered with notes. Some historians believe that the wish to reach Asia directly, without crossing the Mongol lands, was one of the forces that started the age of European exploration.

The main Mongol source for the life of Genghis Khan is the Secret History of the Mongols, a book composed in the thirteenth century whose original text was lost and is known today through a version in Chinese characters. It mixes legend, poetry and plain narrative, and it does not hide its hero's faults, for it tells of killings, quarrels and mistakes alongside the triumphs. Reading it is the nearest that we can come to hearing the Mongols tell their own story.

In 2003 a team of scientists reported that a single male genetic lineage is carried by about eight in every hundred men over a vast area of Asia, which reaches from the Pacific almost to the Caspian Sea. The lineage seems to have begun in Mongolia about a thousand years ago, and some researchers believe that it spread through the male descendants of Genghis Khan and his relatives. Without remains from his grave this can never be proved, and the explanation remains a matter of debate.

In 1924 Mongolia became a communist state, closely tied to the Soviet Union, and the authorities discouraged public admiration for Genghis Khan, whom they described as a feudal lord and a symbol of old nationalism. After the peaceful democratic revolution of 1990, his memory came back into the open, and his portrait appeared on banknotes and his name on streets and companies. In 2006 the country celebrated the eight hundredth anniversary of the founding of the Mongol state.

Today a gigantic stainless steel statue of Genghis Khan on a horse, about forty metres high, stands on the open plain east of the capital, Ulaanbaatar, and visitors can climb inside it to look out across the grassland. Mongolia's main international airport has been named after him, and so have schools, streets and many companies. For a small country of only a few million people, he is the very symbol of national pride.

Many families in Mongolia still live in gers and move their herds through the seasons, as their ancestors did, and the horse is still honoured as a companion of the family. Every July the country holds the national festival of Naadam, in which men and women compete in wrestling and archery, and children, some of them barely old enough to read, race horses across the open grassland. The old life of the steppe has not disappeared, and many people are determined that it should not.

In the lands that the Mongols attacked, including Iran, Iraq, Russia, Ukraine, Hungary and large parts of China, many people remember the conquests with sorrow, and stories about the destroyed cities have been told for centuries. To them the name of Genghis Khan means burning libraries, ruined canals and families that were never seen again, and nobody has the right to tell them to forget it. Honest historians must give those memories the same weight as the stories of achievement.

The Mongol story endures precisely because it holds two truths at the same time, a world that was joined together and a world that was wounded, and each generation has to weigh them again. In Mongolia Genghis Khan is honoured as the founder of the nation, while in the lands that his armies attacked the memory is far darker, and a fair historian must hold both views. It began with an abandoned boy on a sea of grass, and it changed the course of the world.
